subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF UNITED NATIONS UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that today is the thirty-third anniversary of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights and that Canada is one of the foremost supporters of that Declaration, having ratified the International Covenant on Civil and Human rights which gives legal expression to that declaration; and in view of the continuing abuses of human rights in almost all parts of the world by both left wing and right wing regimes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist), the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) and the hon. member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith):
That this House condemn human rights abuses and urge all states to conform to the norms set out in the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and to ratify the International Covenant on Human Rights.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF UNITED NATIONS UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
It is a signal honour which permits me to speak to this most important and timely motion.
Nothing in all of man's activities can even closely parallel in value those efforts put forth in response to human need wherever it occurs. No emotion can possibly equal the emotion involved in feeling at one with fellow men anywhere in the world who suffer individual or national abuse. No calling is of demonstratively more worth than the devotion to respect for human rights in our community, in our nation, and throughout the world.
No single occurrence should inflame our impatience, rebuke our indifference and galvanize us to action more than the oppression of man's spirit and the denial of man's freedoms. In this respect, we are our brother's keeper. Dr. Sakharov in response to Dr. Shcharansky's ordeal said:
Shcharansky represents us all.
This is never more true than when applied to all who suffer from national breaches to human rights.
There is no cause on earth more worthy of our attention as parliamentarians, more demanding of our vigilance, more precious in the sight of God and of man than that cause which pursues as its ultimate goal the enhancement of human and spiritual values and dignities. Wherever abuses occur in Canada, in Europe, in Africa, in Asia, in South America, it is man's spirit that is oppressed, the very substance of humanity which is threatened.
Favoured Canadians generally are the poorer for a lack of real appreciation for the value of human dignity. This lack of understanding results from being part of a most favoured society in a most blessed land, and this sheltering environment breeds a complacency which too easily absorbs us.
Canada has ratified the United Nations International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights which gives legal expression to the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Canada has acceded as well to Article 41 of the Covenant which allows a state, signatory to both the Covenant and the Article, to bring to the United Nations Human Rights Committee a charge that another "state party" has violated its obligations under the Covenant. Most significantly, Canada has ratified the optional protocol to the Covenant which recognizes the right of individuals to bring such charges to the Human Rights Committee. To date, only 12 of the 61 states

December 10, 1981
which have ratified the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights have acceded to Article 41.
Dr. Andrei Sakharov has said that "without human rights there is no detente ... no peace". That is true of nations and it is true of the individual. God grant that even we in Canada will have no peace-no personal peace-so long as the human spirit is denied liberty anywhere in the world. Dr. Sakharov also said that "the price of exercising your rights may well be imprisonment". That, indeed, has been his experience. May we, to the extent possible, share in his suffering.

Canada has today, with the support of all provinces and territories, deposited at the United Nations its instrument of ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women.

subsubtopic: EFFECT ON RETIREMENT INCOME
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my questions today are for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The minister will know that members on this side of the House are very much concerned about people who have recently retired or are about to retire, because the November 12 budget greatly hurt many of those people.
Does the minister think it is fair that those Canadians who have spent a lifetime planning for their retirement by putting their money into a small business such as a farm, a fishing boat or a truck, should have part of that income they were counting on for retirement suddenly taken away on November 12? Does the minister think it is fair to take away part of the income of those who get severance or retirement pay, leaving them with less to live on in their retirement years? Would the minister tell us whether or not she thinks that is fair, and whether she has figures in her department which would indicate how many of these people may now have to be supported at least in part by the tax system in the future?

IMPACT ON PENSIONS AND GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister responsible for senior citizens and retired people has not really given the budget the kind of scrutiny that she perhaps should have before going to cabinet meetings.
In our system, those who work for the government or for a large company such as Imperial Oil, or the Bank of Canada, may belong to a pension plan. They can put quite a bit of their own money and their employers' money into it. But Canadians such as waitresses, cab drivers and others are stuck with trying to put their money into something like an RRSP. Those who are rich in society can put more in than can those who have no company pension plans. I would like to ask the minister if she thinks that is fair and what impact that might have over the long term for her department, respecting the pensions and guaranteed income supplements it must pay.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Labour. He will know that there are some 46,000 employees of airlines who receive a substantial travel benefit which is about to be taxed as a result of the budget. Similarly, there are 100,000 railway workers who have free travel, and that is about to be taxed. This free travel is the result of collective agreements. There are thousands of clerks and other employees throughout the country who work, for example, at Eaton's or Simpsons, and get a 20 per cent discount on sales. There is going to be an irresistable demand in future labour negotiations for inflationary and substantial pay hikes to compensate for the loss of these benefits because of taxation.
Will the minister acknowledge that there will be these irresistable demands for inflationary pay hikes? Second, will the minister prevail upon the Minister of Finance to abandon this particular proposal, which is both unrealistic and counterproductive?

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State. The number one priority recommendation of the Standing Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped for action during the International Year of Disabled Persons was, and I am quoting:
That physical and mental handicaps be made a proscribed ground for discrimination for all discriminatory practices listed in the Canadian Human Rights Act.
In view of the fact that this same recommendation was accepted by the government and included in the Speech from the Throne, and today we are observing International Human Rights Day, would the Secretary of State choose this auspicious occasion to practise what he preaches and assure the House that the required legislation will be on the Order Paper before Parliament adjourns for the Christmas recess, so that arrangements can be made for speedy passage?

the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. It concerns the $94 million which this department squandered through the Enterprise Development Program's guaranteed loans to Consolidated Computer Corporation and its two leasing companies. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the same minister who spent a lot of time telling us all the things he does in research and development. I would like him to cast his mind to his other portfolio, forestry. I would ask him what he has done lately for the forest community, particularly in exercising his clear responsibility to assist the industry, which is in very deep trouble, with research and development.
More particularly, what has he done lately to advance the idea of a regional forest complex for the maritime provinces, an idea which has been on the drawing boards for eight years and has been before the cabinet for eight months? Particularly, what has he done to combine this forest complex with a forest ranger school to overcome some of the serious manpower shortages in this important sector of our economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S ACTIONS TO ASSIST INDUSTRY AND ESTABLISH MARITIME RESEARCH COMPLEX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are a whole series of questions contained within the hon. member's one question. He knows very well that at the end of September we brought forward a discussion paper outlining the problems in the forestry industry in Canada and possible approaches to those problems. We are pursuing the initiatives we took at that time in discussions with the provinces in relation to reforestation. We are bringing forward for government consideration a variety of proposals in relation to marketing, in relation to assistance to the forestry schools of the country, and in relation to the training of highly qualified manpower in the forestry industry.
We do have under active consideration the question raised concerning the Maritime forestry complex, and I expect to be able to make an announcement some time within the next few days.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
That this House censures the government of its perpetual, excessive, and ineffective reliance on a high interest rate policy, which has not only created the worst economic recession in Canada since the 1930s, but which also continues, to threaten the survival of thousands of small enterprises, adds more Canadians daily to the ranks of the million already out of work, and confronts home owners and renters alike with the worst housing crisis since the Second World War.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as we approach the time of the Christmas adjournment the country finds itself locked into a mood of economic uncertainty, critically high unemployment, record high inflation and the worst housing crisis since the Second World War. We have a government that does not seem to appreciate this or in fact want to do anything about it, or respond in any way whatsoever.
The Toronto Sun in its edition dated September 16, 1981, had this headline: "Grits dine as riot cops stand guard". That, of course, had to do with the shameful and disgraceful performance of the minister responsible for housing and his colleagues who called out the RCMP riot squad to shield them from a delegation of irate home owners who were in Ottawa at the time protesting the high interest rates policy. Another headline in the Toronto Star on the same day read: "Home Owners Roll into Ottawa Protesting High Interest Rates".
I refer again to The Citizen published in Ottawa on Wednesday, September 16, 1981-this is very relevant to what I want to say, sir- which carried the headline: "Hang in there, home owners told". It went on:
Grit your teeth and hang on until the federal budget if you are in danger of being foreclosed, Public Works Minister Paul Cosgrove advised home owners Tuesday, holding out promise that help is on the way.
Finally, going back to that September 16 date, I quote from the Toronto Star, which is not unknown to be favourable to the government and not known to misquote any members of the government. The article reads:
Canadians are fed up with the federal government's handling of the economy, particularly high interest rates. Liberal MPs and Senators from across Canada have told Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau and his government.
Those headlines are very relevant with respect to the debate today. It is because of what I and many people construe to be the advance billing by the minister responsible for housing
wherein he raised expectations, deliberately and cruelly, by having us believe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) would be addressing problems facing home owners and renters in the budget as a result of the high interest rate policy, that I intend to focus my remarks particularly on the housing problem.
Let us examine the facts. The housing crisis can best be summarized under two headings, affordability and availability. My colleague the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott) will be dealing with another aspect of the housing crisis with respect to those unfortunate Canadians who have urea formaldehyde foam insulation in their homes. They are the untouchables. They do not even qualify for a conventional mortgage and cannot sell their homes.
I would like to deal with the question of affordability and availability, which has created the worst housing crisis since the Second World War. It has created an acute shortage of rental accommodation in this country, unknown since the Second World War.
If we examine the record, we find that the fact is that in Canada we are just not producing enough new housing units each year to meet the housing needs of Canadians. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada predict that we need, on average, 220,000 new housing units each year to meet this demand. If we examine the record, starting in 1977 housing requirements as compared to housing starts showed a critical decline. At no time since 1977 have we been able to keep up with housing requirements or the demand for housing. For example, in 1977 we needed 256,000 starts and in fact only 245,000 were produced. The number goes down correspondingly. In 1978 the requirement was 259,000 and there were 227,000 actual starts. That continues to the critical period we are in today, 1981, where we required 265,000 starts and only produced 170,000.
If we take the predictions of the minister responsible for housing, the advice he has given his cabinet colleagues, then we are looking at housing starts in 1982 of 135,000 whereas the actual requirement for 1982 is 261,000 units. There is a serious crisis and a critical situation in the country.
Because of the acute shortfall in housing starts, the price of the average Canadian home, which is now $76,000 if you consider an average Canadian home to be a three-bedroomed bungalow, will continue to rise. We are told that we can look forward to increases in the range of 20 per cent next year, once again because of the shortfall and because of inflation. Now, if we are to regard the crisis in that context, what is the response of the government? What advice did the minister responsible for housing have for the people of Canada? This is what he said to his cabinet colleagues, and I quote from the famous leaked document entitled "Impact of Prolonged High Interest Rates on the Housing Sector."
They-

December 10, 1981
High Interest Rates
compares with average investor carrying cost of $750 on the mortgage and property tax for a newly constructed unit with a 30 per cent downpayment.
Again I go on to quote from the document:
Rental investment will thus dry up in most markets. Even when vacancy rates have dropped to zero, there will be no new building until there is a better correspondence between investor costs and market rents for new units. This correspondence will only be achieved after a period during which waiting lists prevail and tenants have little choice of accommodation. Vacancy rates in most markets will approach zero by 1983.
We are almost there. We are almost at zero vacancy rates in most of the major metropolitan areas of the country. The city of Oshawa already has a zero vacancy rate. The city of Toronto has a 0.4 per cent vacancy rate; it is rapidly approaching zero. We can go across the country to the city of Winnipeg, the city of Calgary, the city of Vancouver or the city of Halifax. This is a very, very serious problem, and the situation will get worse.
What is the consequence of this? Again, sir, I have no better authority than the minister responsible for housing, who said:
A black market could develop in rental accommodation with the phenomenon of key money becoming prevalent.
For those who do not understand the term "key money", let me explain. It is a term which came about during the Second World War. It grew from the critical shortage of rental accommodation in many of the major metropolitan areas across the country. You nod, Mr. Speaker, probably because you have first-hand experience. That was the practice whereby, if you were desperate for accommodation, you would bribe the doorman or the building superintendent. In exchange for that bribe he would show you the accommodation available in the building. In return for another bribe he would provide you with a key and a lease. Of course, the understanding was that you would have to provide a bribe every month you were a tenant in that building. That is key money, and that is where we are heading. That is what the minister is predicting. That is the housing black market the minister referred to in his advice to the cabinet. That is a disgraceful situation for a country like Canada.
I want to continue to quote the minister because this is important. I am quoting from a document which was the minister's advice to his cabinet colleagues in trying to make a case for some relief in the budget, which we did not get:
The prospect is not only for tight rental markets but for waiting lists and doubling up with family and friends. We will thus witness a substantial regression in housing conditions following 35 years of gradual improvement.
What a shocking statement. What an indictment out of the mouth of the minister of housing of this government's inability to face up to its responsibility to Canadians. It is interesting that 10, maybe 11 years ago, the minister of housing of the day felt so strongly about the trends in housing in Canada and where we were heading in terms of housing and urban renewal that he put a task force on the road which he himself headed. I refer, of course, to the Hon. Paul Hellyer. When he brought in the report of the task force and its recommendations, he expected some action from the government. When the government failed to act, he did the only honourable thing he could do: he resigned his position from the cabinet.
I suppose you can liken the recommendations in the minister's task force report of ten years ago to the recommendations or warnings contained in the present minister's document to the cabinet of a few short months ago. I suggest to the minister of housing that he would do well to emulate the honourable course of his predecessor, the Hon. Paul Hellyer, and resign from the cabinet.
I advise hon. members who are interested in this crisis, as I am sure all hon. members are, to take a look at the report of the Hellyer task force on housing. They will find it very interesting reading. Many of its recommendations are very relevant to the present housing situation. There were ten principles listed in the recommendations of the task force. I will just quote two which happen to form the keystone of our philosophy as a party. I quote:
Housing and urban development are an urgent priority for the people of Canada and must be treated as such by their elected representatives at all levels.
What a pity the government refused or failed to respond to that recommendation ten years ago. I quote the second principle of the Hellyer task force, one to which my colleagues and I subscribe:
Every Canadian should be entitled to clean, warm shelter as a matter of basic human right.
That is the keystone of our commitments. It is interesting to note that the minister's executive assistance at that time had a large part to play in the drafting of that report. I would not be at all surprised if he had a hand in some of the recommendations.
Hon. members will be interested in knowing who the minister's executive assistant was at that time. He was none other than Mr. Lloyd Axworthy, who now sits opposite as the minister responsible for employment and immigration. He seems to have lost his concern based on his experience. I quote from Hansard of 1979:
The people of Canada are not being crucified, they are being hung, drawn and quartered by high interest rates.
I wish I had said that. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) said that in this House in 1979 when he was the housing critic. He said that at a time when interest rates were at 14 per cent. At 14 per cent he stood in this House and said that the people of Canada were being hung, drawn and quartered. Today we have seen interest rates reach as high as 22 per cent and we see the minister who made that statement now sitting in the cabinet.
What could the government have done? They could have swallowed their pride and reintroduced our mortgage and property tax credit plan. They could have increased the capital cost allowance from 5 to 10 per cent which would help to bring down building costs. They could have continued the MURB program. They could have brought in a shelter allowance to help ease the critical situation in the area of social housing. We do not hear enough about that. All you have to do is read the metropolitan papers of the country to find that the chari-
December 10, 1981

table institutions can no longer cope with the critical demand of those who are literally on the street at night.
The government could have brought in a plan whereby the registered home ownership savings plan could be folded into an RRSP and applied to home ownership. They could have done all those things. There were a number of things they could have done if they fully appreciated the seriousness of the situation in the country today and the depth of feeling of Canadians.
All we get from this government is advice from the minister of housing that Canadians have to lower their expectations. That is the advice of the minister of housing. We have to go back to the way things were two or three decades ago. Tell the young people of the country to make do with orange crates. You will find it awfully difficult to sit on an orange crate today because they are no longer made of wood; you would find yourself with your bottom on the floor in no time short. Yet that is the advice we get from the minister.
I say this to the minister. He was not entirely out to lunch on that advice because the situation 20 years ago was a lot better than it is today. If twenty years ago you could not afford to buy a house because you did not have the down payment and you were just starting out in married life, you at least had an apartment to go to. Now you have no apartment to go to. Housing is beyond your reach. It has become an impossible dream. You either have to forgo your plans or double up with your parents. What a shameful situation in this country today.
I believe before too long we are going to see further back-stepping by the government, what we in Newfoundland used to call turkey-trotting where you take one step ahead and two steps backwards. We have already seen one step backwards when they had to reinstitute the soft cost provisions of the MURB program to accommodate those units which had been started during this current calendar year. I predict that the situation is going to get so bad that before the winter is over this budget, which is already in scrambles, will have to be scrapped.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of this motion with a great deal of pleasure. The effects of the high interest rate policy of this government are now well known. They are even well known to the members on the backbenches opposite in this House of Commons. They cannot ignore the reality that in the past 90 days 140,000 Canadians have lost their jobs through lay-offs. They cannot ignore the reality that 7,000 small businesses so far this year have gone into bankruptcy.
The backbenchers opposite cannot ignore the fact that bankruptcies of small businesses in Canada in November this year compared to November last year were up 49 per cent. That is significant because, as all business people and consumers know, if there is any possibility of staying in business you sure stay in business in November and through the December shopping period. When bankruptcies are up 49 per cent in the
High Interest Rates
month of November this year over last year, it can be seen that we are in the middle of an economic and human crisis.
The backbenchers in the Liberal Party cannot ignore the fact that farmers are being hurt now as never before. I do not need to stress in this House that farmers are hardly well known for demonstrating and actively showing their opposition to government policy when they are unhappy. Of all the segments of our population, they are the small "c" conservative, law-abiding, peaceful group. What have we seen in recent days? In the province of Quebec at St.-Isidore, hog producers block roads. Why? Because of high interest rates and the impact it is having on their operations as farmers. In the Bruce-Grey region of the province of Ontario, another group of farmers have virtually taken to vigilante action to protect their farms from banks and other mortgage holders who may want to take them over.
Finally, as other evidence of the effects of the high interest rate policy of this government, we had the demonstrations just a few weeks ago of 100,000 Canadians who appeared just outside the main door of this building. That figure surprised a lot of people, Mr. Speaker. It surprised me. To be perfectly frank, it surprised the organizers who represented a number of groups. It was almost double the number they anticipated would turn out. They were people who came not simply from trade unions, but small businessmen, home owners, farmers, people who were trying to send a message to the Government of Canada.
Given this reality of 140,000 lay-offs in three months, the record number of small business bankruptcies, the disruption in farm communities, the loss of homes, the fear of renters all over Canada that their rents will increase by two, three or four hundred dollars next year, how have the major institutions with power and responsibility in Canada responded to this?
First we have the Bank of Canada and our beloved Governor, Mr. Bouey. He has seen the reality; he has seen the effects of high interest rates. What has he said? He made a speech a few days ago in which he complained. What did he complain about? He complained about minimum wages. He said that minimum wages in Canada were a source of inflation. He urged the government-I do not exaggerate, these were his words-to hang tough with its policy. That is what the Governor of the Bank of Canada said.

speechtext:
If the Governor of the Bank of Canada's response has been one of ignorance in economics-and I say that bluntly-a failure to understand the economic theory that I thought went out of date at the end of the 1920s or certainly at the beginning of the 1930s and is certainly wrong now, if he is to be faulted for technical competence reasons as well as insensitivity, what can one say about the Government of Canada, which since the Coyne affair at least has had the full legal authority to direct and control monetary policy in this country?
Before I note their reaction, I want to say in passing that even President Reagan of the United States, the arch-conservative of the modern age, has begun to reduce interest rates at a more rapid level in the United States than has the Government of Canada. Even President Reagan has recognized the negative, inhumane effect in terms of escalation of unemployment in the United States that the high interest rate policy has had there.
What we have had in recent weeks is an increase in the spread in interest rates between Canada and the United States. As bizarre as it is in some sense, to contend, President Reagan has had a more humane response to the economic circumstances of the Americans than has the Government of Canada. It is hard to believe, but that happens to be the factual reality.
What did the government do? It had a chance to deal with this reality in the budget, but what does the budget do? The budget continues to tax people who are living on pensions and deliberately creates more unemployment. Its own forecast calculated increases in unemployment for the next three years before there is some turnaround. The only way we will get a turnaround is to turn this government out. But that is in the budget forecast.
It continues to tax pensioners and it deliberately creates unemployment, but at the same time it reduces taxes by as much as $5,000 a year for the very rich in Canada. It is a
government that has responded to budget criticism from its friends, such as Dome Petroleum Limited. It made one phone call and within minutes there was an announced change for Dome Petroleum Limited for its benefit, but we have not yet seen a change that would benefit the poor. It is a budget which, above all at this time because of the government's commitment to interest rates, leaves the truly exorbitant and unconscionable profits of the banks virtually untouched.
I say that in this context of human suffering it is time that the Government of Canada realized that in a democratic society the basic moral obligation of a government is to the ordinary people of the land, not to the rich and powerful who can look after themselves.
Specifically, I want to say something about bank profits. I want to do so for a number of reasons. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in one of his casual and arrogant dismissals a couple of weeks ago when he was questioned about action to improve the wellbeing of the ordinary Canadians, asked: "Where will we get the money?" Then he sat down. That was one of his definitive arguments.
I want to say something about that because the hon. member who sits to his right, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), has said that the banks of Canada must bleed a little. They sure have not been bleeding; they have been leeching the people of Canada. We know their profits are $1.8 billion. Their profits are high. A number of corporations could be having high profits for a variety of reasons. Perhaps some of them are very efficient and are producing a good product that is selling well and producing jobs. There are all kinds of reasons. But the reason the banks are having high profits is made clear not by the New Democratic Party but was made clear earlier this week by a statement from a spokesman for the banks that appeared in a publication of the Canadian Bankers' Association when he said that the reason the bank profits are so high is because of the high interest rate policy of this government.
In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, we say that it is long overdue that we tax the banks at a fair level. That is all we are saying. We are not saying: "Let us confiscate all their revenue, let us seize their property". We are saying that when there are thousands of Canadians living in poverty, when we have a national housing crisis and the highest level of unemployment since the depression, it is time that the banks of Canada did indeed bleed a little and paid their share.
I have a simple proposal to put forward. When the minister responds today, I should like to hear him deal with the argument. Let us tax the banks at a fair level. If they have $1.8 billion, let us levy a tax on them for some $700 million. I am sure the Minister of Finance could figure this out; it would leave approximately $1 billion for the banks. That is not bad, they would still have that profit. We need some $700 million. A few weeks ago the Prime Minister asked from where we could get money to do various things. Go to the banks, go to
December 10, 1981

the banks! Instead of putting it in, take it out for the people of Canada.
Before saying what I would do with it, in this context I move, seconded by the hon. member for Beaches:
That the motion be amended by including after the word "policy" the following:
"and its failure to introduce an excess profits tax on bank profits so that new
programs could be established to assist home owners, and to stimulate
construction of the needed housing units".
What could be done with the results of this single action? There are many other things about which other speakers in my party will be talking today, but I want to zero in on this one item. First, there is a minimal shortage of some 50,000 units for the coming year, even if the projections of the government are lived up to as to what is needed across Canada. With the $700 million which could be obtained if the government acted on this amendment, we would be able to stimulate enough production of housing in Canada to produce the 50,000 units. In addition, at a time when real unemployment levels are in excess of one million, we would be able to produce 110,000 jobs which would result from the construction of the homes, on the one hand, and also from the goods purchased to go in the homes and the services related to the construction of the homes. It would mean 110,000 additional men and women working who want to work; 110,000 men and women would be paying taxes instead of collecting unemployment insurance and welfare. This makes economic and social sense to us. This is a practical and just proposal, a proposal which ought to be implemented right away.
Having made the point about the social sensitivity and economic incompetence of Liberals, I want to turn to the movers of the motion today. If the Liberals have been insensitive to Canadians in the budget, it seems to me that the motion before us demonstrates that at best Conservatives have forgotten their own record and at worst, to be blunt, are hypocritical. I remind the Conservatives present in the House that under the government of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) its monetary policy was precisely the same as that of the Liberal government today.

I hear a Conservative member jeering in the background. Now that they are back in opposition, at least one Conservative member has been consistent. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the former finance critic, said as recently as June in a television interview that he was speaking for his party and that they would support Governor Bouey's high interest rate policy. At least the hon. member has
High Interest Rates
been consistent, but I say to hon. members of the Conservative Party that they cannot have it both ways. They cannot in one motion single out the negative human effects of a ridiculous high interest rate policy and simultaneously advocate a high interest rate policy. The cannot have it both ways.
I conclude my remarks this afternoon by saying that I have repeated in my speech what is well known about the negative effects of the high interest rate policy and the indifferent government. Also in this context I have proposed in a straightforward manner a partial solution to an important problem. If we look at the banks honestly and fairly and make them perform fairly, we could deal with the present housing situation and produce some jobs. This is the precise, concrete action, instead of indifference, which we ought to be receiving from the Government of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I must admit that the amendment proposed by the Leader of the New Democratic Party is a clever one. Throughout his speech, the hon. member failed to address the root of the problem as was the case with the spokesman for the Progressive Conservative Party-and what he is proposing is a band-aid solution. Mr. Speaker, I believe that both the motion and the speeches made in its defence are deceiving, because the official opposition always tells only part of the story. The motion is also false because it does not reflect reality and confuses cause and effect. In addition to being false, it is fallacious, because it creates illusions, is misleading and obscures the real situation by confusing cause and effect. To put it in a medical context, everyone has been discussing symptoms without trying to establish what is really wrong with the patient and prescribing the appropriate medication.
Our main problem-and this was clearly pointed out in the budget-is inflation, which is still very much a fact in our society and in our economy. However, before making alarmist statements, it would perhaps be wise to remember certain facts. For instance, between November 1980 and November 1981, nearly 110,000 new jobs were created in Canada. During that same period, the same twelve months, the economy's real growth was 3.7 per cent. This is, in fact, a remarkable performance compared with the economic situation in the world today. However, although there has been a substantial increase in the number of jobs and the growth rate of our economy, the fact remains that inflation has remained at unacceptable levels, that the unemployment rate is still very high in Canada, and that interest rates are high as well. The government is not saying that the problem is easy to solve, and we are ready to admit that this is a difficult situation. However, we are saying that people should not delude themselves that they will be able to get through this difficult period

December 10, 1981
High Interest Rates
without paying a price. The real enemy to be beaten is inflation. High interest rates are a consequence of inflation and if we really want to bring down interest rates, we shall have to fight inflation and reduce inflationary pressures.
Since the seventies, inflation has become an increasing threat to our economy. Inflation is becoming a way of life. That is the root of the problem, and that is what makes it difficult to solve. We must get rid of our inflationary expectations and at the same time get rid of the causes of inflation. During the last decade, the average inflation rate was 9 per cent. If we look at the decade before that, the average inflation rate was less than 3 per cent. During the seventies, profound changes have unsettled the world economic situation and also our own. For instance, the price of oil products has increased by about 650 per cent. The Canadian dollar has depreciated by about 20 per cent compared with the American dollar. In other words, inflation is a serious problem and it is the problem we must fight. It is no use focusing on external or secondary causes. We must get at the root of the problem, bearing in mind that inflation and inflationary expectations are the cause of high interest rates and are therefore responsible for the consequences of high interest rates.
How borrowers reacted to what they thought were high interest rates this spring and summer is a good example of how inflation affects our behaviour. At that time, when mortgage rates were at a record high-about 16 per cent-housing prices in various areas in Canada, became artificially inflated as a result of speculation. Buyers were willing to pay more, expecting prices to go even higher later on. Similarly, general credit demand did not drop until recently, that is, sometime after interest rates peaked last August. So, instead of blindly concentrating on the issue of high interest rates, it is necessary to understand that as long as inflation stays above 10 per cent, interest rates will not go down. However, interest rates have dropped six percentage points since the month of August. On the other hand, we must realize that there is very little hope there will be a rapid progression in that decline, if inflation does not drop substantially.
What are the alternative suggestions in the main motion and the amendment proposed by the NDP? Would we rather have lower interest rates in the present economic situation? The Bank of Canada could probably take steps to reduce interest rates, but what would the consequences be? There would be a substantial increase in the rate of growth of the money supply. The Canadian dollar would probably drop in value on the foreign exchange market, and that would inevitably lead to a jump in interest rates in subsequent months.
It must be understood that increasing the money supply acts as a two-edged sword. In the short term, it expands credit and reduces interest rates. However, since the money supply is inflated in proportion to economic and production capacity, this creates an inflationary trend, leading to rising interest rates.
It would therefore be inconsistent to abandon a policy that is aimed at bringing down inflation and getting at the root of the problem, just to have two or three months' respite before getting into a situation that is even worse.
Do the supporters of this motion recommend that the government maintain its present monetary policy, while at the same time adopting an expansionary financial policy, increasing its expenditures, setting up new programs and even reducing taxes? That would go against the views of a number of economists who favour reducing the deficit as a means of fighting inflation.
The government recognizes that bringing down the deficit is a major element of the anti-inflation strategy which will alleviate pressures on the capital markets and thus bring about a decrease in interest rates. The alternative policies proposed in the motion now before the House fly in the face of an anti-inflation strategy. Since the supporters of the motion are not likely to really want to give up the fight against inflation, they might prefer that the government impose direct wage and price controls? Such a solution has already been suggested; it was even used temporarily in 1975 and had relatively helpful results in an emergency situation. However, I believe that such controls are generally considered as often resulting in inequity and as failing to strike at the roots of inflation. If opposition members are now suggesting indirectly that we impose wage controls, they should say so, but they should say so openly without trying to undermine the anti-inflation strategy in the eyes of the population. The government could tunnel-vision its approach to inflation as implied by the opposition party by pursuing expansionist policies and developing new programs which would put back for an indefinite period the return to an inflation free economy. In fact, such a tunnel vision would solve nothing and would only delay the solutions which would have to be found sooner or later and would then have to be much more drastic as the situation would have worsened.
In choosing to fight inflation, the government does not want to delude the Canadian people or to give them false hopes. It does not want to mislead the people into believing that inflation is not a problem. As you know, inflation could be compared to obesity. When an individual starts to gain weight, he does not necessarily consider this a major problem, but as he puts on additional pounds, his body loses flexibility and the obese individual will eventually realize that he must radically change his way of life. Of course, there are many degrees in the efforts made to lose weight. An overly drastic diet could make the patient's condition worse. I believe that the same applies to the economy. That is why the government has chosen a gradualist approach, a monetary and fiscal restriction strategy tempered by equity, and indeed an economic policy which fights inflation while avoiding the extremes which would cause more serious damage to those who have problems or which would simply feed the flames of inflation. If we truly
December 10, 1981

want to fight this economic ill which can be compared to obesity, we must reduce inflationary pressures as well as the total demand for goods and services. We believe that this first form of restriction must be applied by the government to its own activities. In 1982-83, the growth rate of government spending will go down to 11.7 per cent, which is lower than the inflation rate.
In other words, if we consider the inflation rate and the rate growth of government expenditures, in real terms there will not be an increase in public expenses. Now what about the reduction of the deficit? The deficit was $13.4 billion in 1981-82, it will be $10.5 billion in 1982-83. As a result of this lower deficit the cash requirements of the government will be lower, and there will be a very significant reduction in the borrowing needs of the government, from $9.8 billion in 1981-82 down to $6.6 billion in 1982-83. The direct consequence of such lower cash requirements next year will enable us to seek less capital on the markets. This partial withdrawal by the government will relieve pressure on interest rates and the declining trend we have been witnessing will continue.
In addition, it will be easier for the private sector to borrow on a less active financial market. This possibility of easier borrowings will pave the way for job-creating investments which will be a shot in the arm of our economy. I mentioned restrictive measures to fight against inflation. I also said that those restrictive measures are being taken while keeping in mind our concern for equity. It was in that spirit that the Minister of Finance announced in his budget speech that he would maintain full tax indexation, the indexation of basic exemptions of the tax rolls as well as the worthwhile indexation of social programs. The 1982 indexation rate will be 12.2 per cent. In terms of purchasing power, the indexation of the tax rolls means that Canadian taxpayers will get refunds in excess of $2 billion.
Therefore, through indexing, the government will be protecting the purchasing power of Canadians in 1982-83, by over $3 billion. It could have ended the indexing of such programs and cut back the deficit by an equivalent amount. But it considers that such a move would have disastrous social effects since the indexing of income tax and social programs is specifically designed to help those who are hardest hit by inflation. The theme of equity upon which, among others, the budget is based will also take the form of selective measures to help those who are hardest hit by high interest rates. Indeed, the Minister of Finance has announced the implementation of a program to facilitate mortgage renewal. The government is prepared to guarantee the terms under which financial institutions will defer part of the interests incurred when mortgage payments exceed 30 per cent of gross income.
Furthermore, in the case of home owners whose mortgage debt could reach unduly high levels as a result of interest deferral, the government proposes to provide assistance in order to reduce or completely eliminate this deferred interest.
High Interest Rates
The government will also be encouraging the construction of rental housing. It will provide interest-free loans of up to $7,500 per unit for 15,000 units allocated to tight markets across Canada. These units will be over and beyond the 25,000 units provided for by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation under its co-operative and nonprofit housing program. The Farm Credit Corporation will also be able to offer loans at 5 percentage points below its normal interest rate through a special $50 million allocation set aside for this purpose.
The budget also contains a series of provisions for small businesses, and these provisions were described yesterday by the Minister of State responsible for small businesses in a very important speech. The government has been selective in distributing aid to various groups in Canada. It would be totally inconsistent of the government to set up subsidy programs for all groups that are affected by present interest rates. Such a policy would be very costly, while feeding inflation as well. On the other hand, if the government were to protect all those affected by interest rates by giving them subsidies, it would not be getting at the cause of our high interest rates and would only provide temporary relief. In fact, giving subsidies to all and sundry would merely create the illusion that our present inflation rate is not serious and that we can go on living as if it did not exist, since the government is going to compensate for high inflation. The government has decided to give selective aid, because inflation and the resulting high interest rates often affect those who can least afford such problems. In fact, the government has introduced the programs I have just described in order to eliminate cases of inequity.
The present monetary and fiscal policies are aimed at deflating inflationary pressures and are involved in a joint effort to reduce inflation. Reducing inflationary pressures is a prerequisite for reducing the high interest rates we are experiencing today. The government cannot fight inflation alone. The strategy for fighting inflation requires all economic partners to make their contribution. High interest rates are a temporary problem if we get at the root of this problem, namely inflation.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the most positive attitude the members of this House could take would be to support the policy of restraint described in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, a policy that is aimed at bringing down inflation and hence interest rates.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this unfortunately timely but very important motion by my friend and colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I wish to focus my remarks on that portion of the motion which deals with the worst housing crisis since the Second World War, and specifically on the

December 10, 1981
High Interest Rates
presence of urea formaldehyde foam insulation in 100,000 Canadian homes and perhaps even more.
The presence of UFFI exacerbates an already critical housing situation. Since we are dealing with this housing crisis, particularly the crisis which affects those unfortunate enough to have had this foam put into their homes, I would like to make an aside here, that I realize it is difficult for ministers and, indeed, all Members of Parliament to be present in the House of Commons on all occasions when there is a crucial debate going on. I think that when the official opposition sets aside an entire day on a matter as crucial as the housing crisis Canada is going through, it would be courteous for the minister responsible for housing to be in his place to be able to hear some of the cases of hardship we want to bring to the attention of the government, and perhaps be able to get some information from the government on what it plans to do to redress these hardship cases.
This government has consigned at least 100,000 home owners, which could mean anywhere from 250,000 to 300,000, maybe half a million, Canadians, to the ranks of the untouchables, the lepers of the housing industry. For a great number of Canadians the presence of UFFI means not only a health crisis and a structural risk-because the unstable product does cause corrosion-but for many, many people it is an economic catastrophe.
My repeated questions in the House over the past few weeks and months on the UFFI matter may have sounded like a broken record, but this Liberal government has broken all records in terms of the home owners' misery index. There will be one million home owners with mortgages coming due this year. About 10 per cent of those home owners will be having genuine difficulty renewing their mortgages, getting them guaranteed, indeed, even trying to sell their homes.
Attempting to answer questions in the House on November 24, the minister for housing, who is responsible in the House for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, stated that nothing has changed with respect to CMHC housing mortgages. However, he failed to point out that CMHC had considered refusing to guarantee mortgages for homes with foam, according to one senior official, but found it necessary to continue insuring them. Then the minister of housing had the gall to suggest to the news media outside the House that it would be prudent of the legal profession and prospective home buyers to find out what kind of insulation is in those homes so as to know whether urea formaldehyde foam is in them.
I would like the minister to tell me who is buying those homes, since he must be aware there are homes in Toronto, Ottawa, Vancouver, St. John's, London, Waterloo, Hamilton, St. Catharines, everywhere in this country, that are not marketable.
Let me read part of a letter, Mr. Speaker, from a home owner in North York, Ontario. This letter is from a large real estate firm and is addressed to Mr. and Mrs. Frank Spitzer, 20 Hilltop Road, North York. The letter says:
You have a lovely home with nicely proportioned rooms, and it is in excellent condition. While it would, under ordinary circumstances, be an extremely
desirable property, and hence very saleable, it is with regret that I must inform you that because of the urea-formaldehyde insulation you had installed, it would be futile for me to take the listing, as there would be little hope of selling it even at a price far below market value.
I am sorry that we cannot do business at this time, but it would be unfair for me to give you false hope about the marketability of your home.
Let me read another letter from Mr. Larry Gee of Point Clair, Quebec. This is from another large real estate firm, A.E. Lepage, and it states:
It is certainly unfortunate that although all of these indications suggest a market value of $42,000.00, I feel that because of the type of insulation (ie urea-formaldehyde foam) in your home it would be virtually impossible to market.
Later in the letter it is stated:
Since the insulation in your home appears to be impossible to remove without virtually removing the building, I would have to consider the building to be worthless. In fact it is a liability, as someone would have to spend money to effect its removal.
The land value in the area indicates that your lot because of its location should sell for $15,000.00; however, the cost of removal of the building may have to be deducted from this amount.
Our office has become sort of an ombudsman headquarters for urea formaldehyde foam home owners across the country. I guess one of the saddest cases has come to my attention through the good offices of the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), from the town of Pelham. There is in Fenwick a senior citizen who has been hospitalized from reaction to the substance UFFI, according to her doctor's findings, and has had to have her home completely reconstructed. My colleague, the hon. member for Erie, informs me that her whole lifetime saving, everything she has right now, is $8,000. The cost to have the foam taken out of her home and to restore it to its original condition was approximately $18,000. This is a senior citizen, and according to the mayor of the town of Pelham, Mr. Bergenstein:
For many, many people, as in the case of Mrs. Illes and several others in my Town, it is presently a personal disaster and I would urge all your respective levels of government to regard it as an emergency and respond appropriately- which means promptly!
That also means positively.
How will these people ever be able to sell their homes? How will they ever be able to obtain mortgages, even if they can afford them, when trust companies and banks such as Canada Trust, the Bank of Nova Scotia and the Toronto-Dominion Bank will not grant mortgages to those who want to buy UFFI insulated homes? In fact, the mortgage insurance companies of Canada will not underwrite any new mortgages on houses insulated with the foam. When the minister suggests that people are buying these homes, I wish he would tell that to the
100,000	home owners who have seen their lives' investments slowly sink beneath their feet.
Most Canadians insulated their homes to save energy costs and conserve the precious resources that we have in this world. About 100,000 to 125,000 home owners insulated their homes with urea formaldehyde foam, 40,000 under the CHIP program. It was a classic case of one arm of the government
December 10, 1981

advising people to use a substance which other arms of government had warned was an unhealthy and unstable product. This is the same government which had recommended its use and eventually banned it altogether as a hazardous product. Because people were concerned about conserving energy, they took the government at its word and insulated with UFFI. Mr. Speaker, I want to stand today and address the opposition motion. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has raised a number of issues in this motion which deserve serious discussion. Unfortunately, when one reads the motion, one is somewhat appalled by one of the shortcomings in it. Perhaps it was not done intentionally and could be amended later on, but the fact is that although the hon. member talks about high interest rates, jobs, housing and the small enterprises of this country, he forgets to mention the root of the problem, which is inflation.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, inflation is running at a very high rate in this country. One of the contributing factors to high inflation is the deficit which this government is attempting to bring under control in a very reasonable way through its recent budget. It is my understanding and belief that by reducing the deficit, inflation will be reduced and will thereby have a direct impact on high interest rates. It should be said that members opposite, whether they come from St. John's East or from Oshawa, are not the only ones, nor are their parties concerned about high interest rates. We on this side of the House are equally concerned and I believe that we have now taken some action which will eventually alleviate inflation, bring it under control and impact upon high interest rates.
We need a lower deficit, Mr. Speaker. A reduction in the deficit will have positive effects over time on inflationary expectations through expenditure restraint and deficit reduction. The federal government is giving a clear signal that it intends to restrain the growth of its demands on the economy.
Another result from reducing the deficit is that the government will reduce its demands on the financial market, thereby making it easier for the Bank of Canada to achieve its monetary growth targets and restrain demands for credit in the economy. A reduction in the deficit, through restraint on government spending and increased taxes, directly leads to reduced demands for goods and services.

One of the criticisms is that investors in small businesses and those who invest in office buildings, factories and apartment buildings will be deterred by the provision restricting deductibility of interest rate expense from investment income.
There are a number of factors which deal with that particular criticism which I would like to state for the record. First, this measure does not deny a deduction. It only changes the timing of it, when it may be claimed. Borrowing costs on one asset may be offset against any investment income that the individual has from assets or other investments. The facts are that if the measure had applied in 1979, over 76 per cent of interest costs would have remained deductible immediately. Of the 1.3 million individuals who claimed the deduction, only
198,000	of them would have had their interest costs limited, and of these, 163,000 would have had their taxable income affected by less than $500. Only 7,000 persons would have had restricted interest expenses of over $5,000. For many of these people the tax rate cut benefits will offset the restrictions in interest expense deductibility.
Of the large number of individuals who invest in risky ventures or securities, most invest their own savings or have adequate investment income in total to be able to claim any interest expense on borrowed funds.
The revenues from this measure are being used to help finance reductions in tax rates which will reduce the top rate on capital gains from 33 per cent to 25 per cent on average and will increase the after tax return on risky investments. We must keep certain policy measures in perspective, and that is one matter on which I want to elaborate today.
The motion today alleges a lack of concern for home owners and renters in this country, but I think the minister responsible for housing as well as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) have provided a sizeable amount of money and directed it in such a way that I hope-and I am sure hon. members opposite hope-will help alleviate some of the hardships Canadians are facing at the present time.
For home owners, growth in income means that most Canadians are able to renew their mortgages by adjusting their spending decisions. But for those facing the potential loss of their homes, the Government of Canada is introducing a program to help. For those home owners whose payments would exceed 30 per cent of their household incomes and who wish to enter into a deferred interest plan with their lending institutions, the government is prepared to guarantee repayment of this deferred interest up to $3,000. For home owners whose payments would exceed 30 per cent of their household income and who have yet to build up sufficient equity in their homes to support interest deferral, the Government of Canada will pay 100 per cent of the interest deferred under the guarantee plan to a maximum of $3,000.
Hon. members opposite have very graciously referred to the measures the Government of Canada is taking in relation to
renters. A number of criticisms of government policies have been made. One particular criticism is that under the budget it will be more difficult for a small businessman to sell his business because it eliminates the so-called reserve provisions and thus imposes tax on capital gains at the time the business is sold, even if the buyer does not pay cash for the full purchase price. The fact in relation to that concern is that, as a result of the reduction in marginal tax rates, the maximum tax on a capital gain will now be only 25 per cent of the gain. The gain itself will invariably be less than the sale price of the business. Thus, the tax will be only a small proportion of the sale price, and the seller would normally receive at least some of the proceeds in cash, which he could use to pay the tax.
The seller may now choose to forward average the capital gain through the new budget provision so that it can be spread out and taxed in later years when his tax rate is lower. This provision will be of significant benefit to those who are selling their businesses on retirement and, with the lower tax rate proposed in the budget, will provide benefits similar to, and in some cases better than, those provided under the IAAC and reserve provisions.
In addition, the pre-budget rules provided a very significant tax deferral advantage to some taxpayers which was not generally available to all. This deferral advantage was of primary benefit to high-income taxpayers. The new forwardaveraging system will allow averaging of the capital gain over many years without also providing tax deferrals which resulted in a few high income individuals totally escaping paying federal tax.
Another criticism was that allowing only one-half capital cost allowance write-off in the year an asset is acquired will reduce the cash flow of small businesses. That, too, is a faulty criticism. The measure thus merely alters the timing of depreciation but not the total amount. The amount of depreciation not allowed in the year an asset is acquired will be deductible in subsequent years. An hon. member opposite is nodding his head in agreement; I am glad he concurs in what I am saying.

that has long outlived its usefulness. And the minister has no new statements to make on the subject, and I must say it is terribly depressing for Canadians who are aware of the situation to listen to this kind of news today, and it is certainly depressing for people like myself who are trying to persuade the members opposite to at least have the guts to tell their Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen): But you have not found the solution yet. However, out of partisanship these people will once again have to support and defend their government tonight, even if they may not be doing so with much enthusiasm. During the budget debate, I was listening to the member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) and to the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) who severely criticized the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). As usual, however, they voted in favour of a budget that is seriously affecting industries in their own ridings, Mr. Speaker.
Once again this evening, the Minister of Finance, who is giving evidence of even greater incompetence than his predecessor, will be applauded. This seems impossible to me, but the Minister of Finance will once again be covered for this evening, and the Minister of State for Finance has given us the same old story that he probably repeats all across Canada but which does not meet our needs or suggest appropriate corrective action. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) is being criticized simply for having shown that our housing policies are clearly inadequate to meet Canadian needs, and not a single government member can deny it. There will be a housing shortage and therefore a major problem in this area, and I am certain that hon. members opposite know as well as I do that there will be a shortage in the coming year. I must therefore congratulate the mover of the motion for having introduced this subject in the House of Commons, and I hope that the government members will force the Minister of Finance to show at least some sympathy for those people who are now or who will be soon without a home. I am not exaggerating, Mr. Speaker. Those are the facts. Some will say: It is not easy. Of course not, but this is the issue we wanted to discuss today in an attempt to convince government members that they should show more human feelings than they have done until now by doing nothing.
The hon. member for St. John's East was quite right to raise this issue in the House. We are not saying that everything in the budget is unacceptable, but certain omissions are inexcusable, and as responsible members of this House and as a responsible party, we want to ask the government to seriously think about such basic necessities as housing. Of course, interest rates have been harmful; they have been fatal to the building industry. The hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Olivier) is aware of it. It is obvious that interest rates have frozen the building industry and put thousands of people out of work. Consequently, there will not be enough housing units for all Canadians. Any self-respecting country or government should
December 10, 1981

be farsighted enough to provide at least this much. Not only are there more and more unemployed in Canada, but there is also an increasing number of people without a home because of an extremely dangerous product-and I shall get back to that later-but the government is doing absolutely nothing to help them except for a few tests with results to be published later. For the moment, some Canadians are without a home for lack of an effective housing policy, and matters have been made even more difficult because of high interest rates, as we must all admit.
The New Democratic Party accused us earlier of having nearly the same views as this government about economics. If the philosophies of our two parties have been somewhat similar, it still remains that on this side of the House, we have been able to make a choice when faced with the need to house Canadians. This is where we must make some choices and establish certain priorities to provide certain advantages to home owners, and this is what we had proposed. In 1982, home owners could have received a credit of $1,500 to help them face the present situation. But this government defeated us on this vitally important question for home owners, and it is important for home owners to realize it, Mr. Speaker. When we made that proposal, I recall quite clearly that our friends opposite blamed us, supposedly because tenants had been forgotten in the home owner tax credit bill. Obviously if this bill could have been implemented, home owners would have been quite embarrassed to talk about increases this year. It is important in my view that the issue be dealt with seriously, that we confront the government with it and urge government members to bring those responsible to their senses. To allow these people, and this is what I am seeking from hon. members on the government side, to advise the ministers of inadequate or unapplied measures, and these people are aware of it, according to the remarks we hear nowadays. speechtext: I am told not to cry over that. I think this is serious, Mr. Speaker. In all those ridings which are represented by government members, the electors put their faith in them. Those men and those women promised they would form a good government, a government of men and women who would show respect for their fellow human beings, but that is not what is happening. We will stand idly by while maybe 25 or 30 per cent of the Canadian population will be living the worst experience of their lives right in the middle of the forthcoming holiday season, Mr. Speaker. We should do everything we can to try and force this government to respond in a more respectful, more charitable and more compassionate way to those groups of people who cannot take it any longer. That, Mr. Speaker, is our problem in Canada right now. Let no one ask me to have faith in a government which has been failing so miserably for the past 15 years, which has inflated its deficit and boosted the number of people out of work; a great many plants are closing down and things are getting worse every day. They bragged about 110,000 new jobs, but they did not say how many jobs had been lost during the same period. We are moving backwards and people are suffering. This is an opposition day and once again I hope-I will not ask for a time extension-I echo from the bottom of my heart, Mr. Speaker, the wishes of thousands of electors in Quebec and in Canada. People tell us that the situation is bad and they wonder what is going to happen. We cannot answer that, but what we do know is that some people will not be able to join the festivities like the others, they will not be able to eat like the others; those are basic rights, Mr. Speaker, but they are being thwarted by an economic policy which has turned out to be a monumental failure. That is clear. Let us reassess our priorities and help the most needy. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Corriveau) agrees with me, I am sure of that, and in his riding as well there are people, farmers who are now worried because problems which should be solved are not being solved, and for the residents of Frontenac as well as those of Joliette I hope they will be solved. I would invite those people to put pressure on the ministers responsible and urge them to find some kind of solution; it may not be a component of an over-all policy but it will have to be modified because the over-all policy falls far short of the mark, something which Quebecers and Canadians, thousands of Canadians, are aware of, just as most members are, here in this House. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the other side has the majority and they would rather glorify a finance minister who shows such incompetence and lack of compassion for the Canadian people.
