subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: The hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that my colleague, the member for Longueuil, will have a chance to rise on a matter of privilege tomorrow to raise the point he wishes to discuss. To the member for Joliette, I would like to say that I find it very stimulating to follow a Frenchspeaking member. It is the first time this has happened to me since I became a member of this House. Unfortunately, I think Quebecers have lost confidence in the Progressive Conservative Party and have never really had any confidence in the New Democratic Party. They do trust the Liberals, which is good for the province but makes it less interesting for us Liberal members, since we never have a chance to answer a francophone member when we take the floor.
Before discussing the motion introduced today, I will start with the small fry, the rump of the House, the New Democratic Party. I was listening just now to the eloquent speech by the Leader of the New Democratic Party who was launching his strongest arguments against the government's budget, its mortgage rate policies, and against every conceivable fault the government might have.
It seems that the Leader of the New Democratic Party is against the budget policy and the mortgage rate policy of the Liberal government. If he does not agree with the government, why wasn't the Leader of the New Democratic Party in the House on December 8 when we voted on the budget, in order to vote against it. I think this neatly characterizes the party. I am against but I will not vote against, or I am in favour but I will not vote in favour. Or else, I am voting in favour, but I am against, or I am voting against, but I am in favour. The epitome of indecision! A party that includes, among its members, people with a negative outlook, highly trained intellectuals who are supposed to bring this country to a certain kind of socialism which is not clearly defined and which flirts from time to time with communism, when their leader is meeting international communist parties or other kinds of communists when he is travelling in Salvador. We do not need that kind of
High Interest Rates
party! We do not need them because Canadians will not build a country for the future with that kind of help. I am very serious about this because for a long time, for 18 months, I have been watching this party that has no face of its own-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Tell us about the unemployed in Lac-Saint-Jean. Talk some sense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I tell people who voted NDP in the last election to look at the vote on the budget on December 8, 1981, and they will realize that the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party was not present. That is further proof that that party is a no-decision party. When it is time to take action, they are not present.
[ Translation]
That is simply unacceptable. I also have a few words for a friend of the New Democratic Party, the leader of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. McDermott, who likes to visit Parliament Hill and who, as the leader of Canadian workers, is doing more than anyone else to harm their cause. Mr. McDermott is no longer a union leader, Mr. McDermott is now a politician-a politician doing what? He makes workers go on strike and lose money, and he comes here to support a political party that is decadent, has no positive contribution to make and would have us believe that it represents the workers of Canada. No, Mr. Speaker, we do not need such allies because the real challenge of this country will be to rebuild for the future. When we speak about inflation and high interest rates, what does it mean? It means aging industries. We need a new economic structure. There is sometimes talk of renewing our labour structure and relations. Can Mr. McDermott help us reorganize labour relations and find positive solutions? Certainly not! He has always clearly stated that he wants nothing to do with the government, that he is there to fight and that he is simply acting as a messenger of the New Democratic Party to try to manipulate workers so that they will vote for that party even though he never succeeds. This is something that I wanted to mention.
As for the motion introduced by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), this is what we find in the first few lines:
That this House censures the government of its perpetual, excessive, and ineffective reliance on a high interest rate policy, which has not only-
-and so on. Strangely enough, when we have these opposition days, no constructive suggestion is ever made saying, for instance, we, of the Progressive Conservative Party, would like to work with the Canadian government to bring solutions to the problems facing Canadians. Why are we being censured? The government of Canada is being censured because the dollar has not gone down by one cent in the last year in Canada while the currency has gone down by 20 per cent, 25 per cent and 30 per cent in the countries who form the Europe

December 10, 1981
High Interest Rates
of the nine and who are saying: There are nine of us and we are strong enough to resist the pressures of American interest rates. Who pays the bill when a currency goes down by 20 per cent, 25 per cent, and 30 per cent? How much would it cost to purchase ordinary consumer goods, such as automotive parts, oil, and everything that we import like sugar and steel, if our dollar had fallen by 25 per cent in 1981? Who is the hardest hit in such a case? Not the millionaire! It makes no difference to the millionaire if gas costs $2 or $4 a gallon. It makes no difference at the end of the month. It only means lower taxes.
But for the poor, the unemployed, the person on welfare, what would their position be if the dollar went down by 25 per cent like the French franc has done or even like the great German mark, which has suffered an incredible fall last year? These countries have tried to follow another policy than that which was needed in the interest of the population. They believed that the nine countries together were strong enough to withstand the import of American interest rates. Just look at the result. I believe that we have to realize, Mr. Speaker, that when we speak of interest rates in Canada, only the rich can afford to borrow. Do not try to borrow if you do not have any money, Mr. Speaker. If you try it, the bank will tell you: Even at 2 per cent, you will not get a loan. The rest of the population is forgotten.
I heard the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) speak earlier about over one million unemployed. Yes, but are you forgetting them? Ask those people if they are able to borrow, even at 2 per cent! Those are the people the government is protecting by telling the others: Even though for a while interest rates are higher, and you are facing the impact of a difficult policy to support our dollar, in so doing you are supporting your children because most of the time, unfortunately, the children of people with money do not work. The father has a job, a good income but the son is unemployed. This is the problem we are confronted with, because of our obsolescent factories, because of job security, because provincial governments, such as the friends of the honourable member for Joliette, put forward legislation as the one under which there must one apprentice for every five journeymen. How is it possible to think this opens opportunities for the young, Mr. Speaker? One apprentice for every five journeymen! No! What this government is trying to do is helping the people and getting allies to do so. And how are people going to be helped? The way the recent budget is doing.
Currently, farmers are entitled to the Small Business Development Bond program. This is one way of helping them. Those in difficulty are entitled to a five per cent rebate on the rate charged by the Farm Credit Corporation. And anyway, that rate is going to be revised downward as early as the end of December, and we are told that this five per cent rebate will be maintained. There have been many benefits: housing construction in areas where there is a need, the government will have build 7,500 new units.
People who are in danger of losing their homes, and I would like to say to my colleagues that I helped some of them recently, can now apply to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The government will help them to keep their homes. We are intelligent enough to realize that it would be costlier to build new ones instead of keeping those which are already there, We are not that stupid. However, I heard a while ago the speech of the member for Joliette and I thought that such a speech would have been more appropriately delivered not in this House but in the legislature where he tried to be elected. When the member said that Montreal was losing its international status, I found it strange because five years ago Montreal was still the metropolis of Canada but it now appears that it is no longer the case. Five years ago, Montreal was still an international city, the proof given being the Olympic Games of 1976. Why is Montreal no longer an international city? For the simple reason that during the past five years the government has done nothing to help Quebecers, but is only interested in one thing, and we were again aware of this during the weekend, to build a new country at any cost and it was the party in power, the Parti Quebecois, which during the weekend held its national convention Mr. Speaker. How long did they discuss the Quebec economy in the plenary meeting at that eighth annual convention? I give you a thousand guesses: They did not for one minute, not one second. Is not that weird? But that's the way things go under that government.
The government is trying to find partners to help it to solve the problems of Canadians. I heard the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) say that we had not done what should have been done to help as far as housing and interest rates on mortgages are concerned. Can anybody tell us what the Saskatchewan government has done? Neo-Democrats are allegedly socialists, but what have they done to help poor home owners? Nothing. I am eager to see what the new Manitoba government will be doing and I remember, I still go farther than those so-called socialists, that not so long ago, they were still discussing there whether the equality of sexes would be recognized.
One of the two premiers who dug in his heels up to the very end was Mr. Blakeney, a member of the New Democratic Party in Saskatchewan. What kind of socialism is that? And the great discovery these governments have made, and I include the government of Quebec, because everybody in Quebec has heard this for the last five years, they have discovered that whatever goes wrong, the federal government is to blame. We, the provincial governments, are elected but we have no powers; you elect us for the sake of tradition because you have to have a leader, but all the power is in Ottawa.
Well, I have the impression that people are starting to get the message, but it is not exactly what they meant to say. The message is, I think, that when something positive is done such
December 10, 1981

as health insurance legislation, access to post-secondary education, hospital insurance legislation, it is initiated by the Canadian government which tells the provinces: This is what you are going to do to improve the wellbeing of your citizens. People are starting to understand, and I am reminded of the people in Montmagny who are having all kinds of problems as a result of the economic situation. And whom do they ask for help, whom do they ask to make their region a designated area? Not the members of the government of the province of Quebec, they know they won't do anything to help them. Those people are only interested in one thing, their nation and their flag. What happens to Quebecers does not interest them in the least. They went directly to the Canadian government which has proved, and is continuing to do so, that it is interested in taking action and helping individuals to develop in a liberal sense and to live without constraints in this country. It is really nonsensical that the opposition parties in this House should join the provinces in telling us that everything that goes wrong in Canada is the federal government's fault.
I would like to draw the attention of my hon. colleagues to the fact that there are several Conservative governments in place in other provinces. What are they doing to improve the economy? I will tell you what they are doing. The Premier of Newfoundland is very willing to come to Ottawa to sign agreements with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) when the federal government foots 90 per cent of the bill. But what kind of a budget do they fish out of their fertile little imaginations? Right now there are all sorts of suggestions and speculations being made over the fact that the Canadian government, through its budget, is hitting hard at this or that group, but that completely ignores the fact that 12 million Canadians will be paying less income tax next year.
Now, life insurance. What a terrible thing it is to defend the insurance companies, which pay 4, 4Vi or 5 per cent interest. If you pay $25 or $30 a month in insurance premiums, at 4'A or 5 per cent interest, it would take you an awful long time to reach the first $1,000 tax deductible. This will never be taxable. We are accused of the worst sins under the sun. The best advice I would be willing to give to my constituents, Mr. Speaker, would be for them to borrow on their life insurance, since they would get a loan rate of 6 or 7 per cent, which comes up to about the same as they get from the companies. That is one way of beating the high cost of money. The money is there, it belongs to everyone and anybody can borrow his or her own money at a normal rate, that is at a rate which allows the company to make a certain profit and which is related to the yield that money has produced for the individual.
Members opposite find this quite amusing of course because any constructive proposal makes them laugh. They are not here to represent their constituents, they are here to fling abuse at the government. They completely ignore the fact, for instance, that Canadian farmers, dairy farmers, have told the
High Interest Rates
government: "We think you have a good, an excellent dairy policy; let us have it for another five years. And it is very good". Members opposite would never dare tell that to their constituents. It would be sinful to say that the government has a good policy, because it would be awful to have to tell everyone the truth. That is the kind of attitude which undermines this country, which is responsible for the fact that we have a leader on the other side who is just an immature politician who is merely concerned with making trouble, having fun at the expense of everybody else, showing through childish antics that he is still the best.
What is even worse, and what I cannot fathom, is that after Canadians have told him that they wanted him no longer as their Prime Minister, that nine months had been long enough, that the labouring pains had been too unendurable and that the pregnancy had been too unbearable, the people who sit behind this man continue to endorse him. That is unbelievable! What will Canadians have to do to show them that they do not want their leader? Perhaps send them a series of telegrams or ask Mr. McDermott to come back, but this time to support his NDP colleagues against the Leader of the Opposition. That may be a solution for he enjoys travelling around. He cannot find time to review his files, but he does get around. That may be a solution.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Let's have an election!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Yes, an election. Let us talk about elections. Mr. Speaker, those people simply love elections. They were in office and could have stayed there for four years. They introduced a budget and said: The Liberals are bluffing, they will not vote against us, we will have them approve a budget as if we were in a minority position and, at the worst, we will call an election and do as the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker once did-after nine months we will be in a majority position. The people got the picture, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the members of the opposition got the picture as well: Canadians do not elect governments to call elections, they elect governments to look after the administration of their country. An election is a democratic tool, not something everybody enjoys because it gives him or her an opportunity to go on a campaign. We should not think that Canadians enjoy the fun of listening to politicians talking through their hats and making speeches here and there. No. Canadians accept the fact that politicians do exist and want to talk to them now and then, because they need people to administer their country.
Fortunately this country goes on growing, expanding and developing, showing ever more respect for the individual citizen regardless of his or her language, colour, race and religion; Canadians have been fortunate over the past 20 years because the Liberals have been in power in their country. The only thing I ask from the people is that they understand the nature of political liberalism. I would strongly urge them to elect Liberal governments in the provinces so that we will no longer

December 10, 1981
High Interest Rates
be alone to work for the wellbeing of Quebecers and of the other citizens of this country, so that we will have allies whose sole objective will be not to promote their own credibility or prove that they wield more power than the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). Let us elect Liberals everywhere in this country and we will see that problems such as the ones we have today will be much fewer and we will come up with solutions to help the most disadvantaged people come to grips with all those problems.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the advantages of having a Christmas break is that the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimatel) will be able to return to his riding to face the truth. He will have to face the unemployed and he will have to face the hardship that people are experiencing caused by high interest rates. He will have to face the cost of this stupid, incompetent budget, the kind of incompetence that was expressed this afternoon by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres). When hon. members on the other side are away from this place for a month of two, they will have to face what is going on out there.
Last night in Toronto the monetary policy of this government, financed in the green glass tower across the way on Wellington Street and sponsored by this government, was described to members of the Toronto Board of Trade. Over 600 very worried people were there.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: All Tories.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
John Grant from the Toronto-Dominion Bank, who is not necessarily known as a Tory, classified the government's policy as kamikaze monetarism. There was not one economist there who forecast growth for next year. Some economists forecast a 3 per cent negative growth in real terms. The best forecast and the most optimistic was for only 1 per cent negative growth. That is what we have coming.
We have just finished taking a look at the budget which stated that Canada will have a balance of payments deficit of $9.1 billion. No one would forecast that small a deficit in our balance of payments. The current forecasts for this year are for a deficit in our balance of payments of between $11 billion and $12 billion.
Why do we have that state of affairs? Let us go back a little way. When the Progressive Conservative Party took over as the government of this country in June, 1979, the current account deficit for 1979 was forecast to be in excess of $7 billion. As we worked through the fall on improving business confidence, the current account deficit for 1979 turned out to be less than $2 billion. Interest rates were high in Canada during that period of time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: They rose.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Yes, they rose. They rose to 14 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext: They went up four times.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Interest rates rose four times, but they remained lower than the interest rates prevalent in the United States during all of that time. There was confidence in Canada, and the dollar increased in value. But now what do we have? Since this government brought in its National Energy Program last year, there has been a massive outflow of capital from this country. Last year the outflow of capital resulted in a small balance of payments deficit. This year the balance of payment deficit will be nearly $12 billion.
What did we have to do to replace that outflow of capital? We had to go to the banks, the hot money lenders of foreign countries, to borrow, borrow and borrow, and we had to let our interest rates rise higher and higher and higher.
Let us take a look at where interest rates are today. The Americans can place T-bills on their market at 10.3 per cent. We placed our T-bills on our market today at 14.93 per cent. We pay 4.63 per cent more than the Americans do.
Let us look at what commercial borrowers have to pay on bankers' acceptances. Commercial borrowers in the United States borrow money at 11.6 per cent. Borrowers in Canada pay 16.85 per cent, or 5.15 per cent more interest than borrowers do in the United States.
Let us look at the European Eurodollar market. It costs 12.5 per cent to borrow money on the Eurodollar market. But the prime rate in Canada is 17.25 per cent. Why is that? You can borrow money on the LIBOR market for 12.75 per cent, but the prime rate in Canada is 17.25 per cent.
Yesterday I asked the minister in charge of this debate why he could not do something about this prime rate problem. He said "You have to understand banking. You are too ignorant. You do not know any better".
I want to tell you what is wrong with the government. Business has lost confidence and the banking community cannot borrow money in Canada for any less than about 4 per cent to 5 per cent more than it can in the United States. The government cannot bring American money, European money, German money or money from whatever country to finance loans in Canada cheaper because people do not have confidence in Canada. People are taking their money out of Canada. That is what is happening.
The only way we can keep money in the country is by keeping a high interest rate policy to balance off that horrid balance of payments problem that the government's incompetence has created. It has been created because of the lack of business confidence, first, in the National Energy Policy and second, in this budget.
This budget again attacks business, entrepreneurialship, growth, progress and job creation. Our economy is damaged by political divisiveness in this country. The government is always trying to have a war with the provinces, and now it has one going again with the province of Quebec. Statements coming out of that province are again hurting and driving business and capital from Canada. On the whole front, politi-
December 10, 1981

cal, economic and business, this government is driving money out of the country, and the only way we can keep money in the country is by raising our interest rates higher, higher and higher.
The government says it is doing this to maintain the value of the Canadian dollar. We are maintaining the value of the Canadian dollar all right, but we are maintaining it artificially high, because on any realistic interest assessment on world interest rates, our dollar, unless we are prepared to pay the premium we are presumably being forced to pay, would have declined and declined considerably.
This government tries to hide its incompetence in management by artificially keeping the dollar higher than it would normally be, and that situation will continue if this country is managed the way this government wants to manage it. There is no reason for our dollar to go below 84 cents or 85 cents. Managed properly, there would be an inflow of capital into this country to take advantage of the resources of Canada, the real wealth of Canada, and to make this country grow. Surely there are people who are hungry in the world; surely there are people who need our forest products; surely there are people who want the products we create. They are afraid to come here and create, afraid to come here and develop opportunities. We drive out the people who would explore and develop our energy wealth. We drive them out by expropriating, by double-taxing and triple-taxing them. We tax away entrepreneurialship and then we wonder why we have unemployment. We wonder why people have to pay enormous amounts on home mortgages.
We drive up the value of our currency artificially with our interest rate policy. We do not need to drive it up artificially. Our currency would rise with a decent economic policy, as it did when the Conservative government was in power. With these people in power, we are now paying nearly 5 per cent more than is being paid in the United States for equivalent money.
The government says the high interest policy is needed to curb inflation. How does it curb inflation? I suppose it curbs inflation by driving beef farmers to sell off their herds so that some people can find cheap meat temporarily, or by forcing businessmen into bankruptcy so there are bankruptcy sales. I suppose that is how they do it. I suppose they cut prices down by putting storekeepers out of business so they have to sell off their stock cheap. Maybe you can cut prices that way for a day or two, but the only real way to cut prices is by increasing productivity, and you cannot increase productivity by making it more difficult for a businessman to buy a new piece of capital equipment. You do not increase productivity by making it more expensive for him to raise money. You do not increase productivity by preventing interest from being deductible or by preventing a person from investing, or making it unattractive for him to invest in an insurance policy. That is the kind of thing we have coming from this government. We have a government that is against increased productivity.
What this government says is that it is going to force prices down and force inflation down by increasing interest rates. It says we have to build a new country so it is going to destroy
High Interest Rates
everything we have and then start building everything again from scratch. You do not build by destroying and you do not build by putting people out of business. That is what this government is doing with its interest rate policy. It is putting people out of business and home owners out of their homes.
We wonder why wage rates are high and why we have demands for higher wages. I was talking to the president of International Nickel the other day and he said: You know, our people in Thompson, Manitoba, have been on strike for a big wage hike. I do not know what we are going to do. We will have to pay them more. I do not blame them for wanting more. After all, their mortgage payments have gone up $100, $200 and $300 a month in some cases, so they need more. How do I pass that on in the international nickel market? What can I do about it?
The government says high interest rates cut inflation. I will tell you what they do. They put people out of work and on unemployment insurance. I suppose they think productivity will increase when people are not working and are being paid not to work. The only way to attack inflation is to increase the productivity of the country, to produce more goods and services, and to have more things available, reducing the cost of producing things by using more machinery by more adequate distribution systems and by a better transportation system. Unless we have a government that is prepared to understand that this is the way we have to go, we will always have higher inflation.
As the government raises interest rates, the inflation rate will go up. That is what has happened. The inflation rate this year is higher than ever at 12.7 per cent. That is the highest rate the country has faced in ages. Interest rates are higher than ever. It is true that they are a little lower today than they were in August, but they are higher today than they were a year ago. Has this government done anything about these high interest rates over the years to bring inflation down? Not on your life. Inflation a year ago was running at about 10 per cent, and now it is running at nearly 13 per cent. We have had another full year of high interest rates and kamikaze monetarism. The government wants to destroy the whole system in order to make its theory work, but it is not working. It is about time the government woke up to the fact that it is not working and woke up to the fact that you cannot drive business out of the country, cut down on productivity and expect all of a sudden to improve our inflationary position. Unless these interest rate policies are changed, sir, we are going to have a very hard time in Canada for a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will begin my remarks this evening by referring to the Speech from the Throne, as I have done on a couple of earlier occasions in this session, in speaking on the matter of housing. It was from the Speech from the Throne that the government took its mandate and made certain commitments to the electorate in an expression of that mandate. Some of those commitments dealt specifically with the issue of housing. I will quote these words, which deal clearly with the issue of housing, saying that the government would:
.. . act to assist those unable to bear the burden of renegotiating their home mortgages in the present abnormal situation so that the spectre of foreclosure will be avoided.
It was an undertaking that we, as a government, would act in these abnormal circumstances to prevent foreclosure. As I indicated, that was the undertaking and that was the action taken by the government in the budget provisions. We have done exactly what we said we would do. We have introduced, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) the Canada mortgage renewal plan which was designed specifically to respond to our undertaking as a government.
There has been criticism in the last few days of the design of the program. One criticism has been that we have not offered enough funding for the program. The Leader of the New Democratic Party has called for an expenditure of $750 million. He stated that we have not really met our undertaking. However, as I have indicated, the program is designed to implement what we have undertaken. It is a two-part program, a deferral of interest and a grants provision. The deferral of interest provision is a design feature of the program whereby those people who have sufficient equity in their homes are able to draw upon that equity to assist themselves, but with the assistance of the federal government backing the financial institutions across the country, thus enabling Canadians who heretofore were not able to use that device to avoid foreclosure by deferral of interest to a point where interest rates, as we all hope, will be lower than they are now. Certainly we hope they are at a lower level than they were during the months of August, September and October.
The other part of the program is the grants provision. It is part of the program that recognizes the difficulties for Canadians who have newly-acquired homes and who have entered into home ownership plans recently and have not built equity or have gone into home ownership in some markets where the equity in the home or the value of a particular project has not increased and they are unable to respond to their problems. In those cases where interest deferral does not apply, the government will provide an outright grant of up to $3,000 to assist those people who apply and qualify under the terms of the Canada mortgage renewal plan.
As well, the budget addressed a problem which has been raised by many members of the House. I would respectfully submit that it was raised by me early this summer in material prepared for my cabinet colleagues in which I expressed my concerns about the housing situation in Canada and envisaged where the concerns and the hazards would be the greatest in the next few years. After identifying the priorities in our concerns, the Minister of Finance responded by supporting the construction of modest rental accommodation across the country in those markets which have the lowest vacancy rates at the present time.
There is also support available for the construction of rental accommodation in areas where Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation local officials and provincial ministers and their officials identify specific needs and anticipated growth, and in areas where it is obvious that rental accommodation will have to be supplied to meet specific circumstances. For that reason, the Minister of Finance introduced through the budget the provision of $350 million in funding for the Canada rental supply program. I had the opportunity of explaining these two programs to the provincial ministers of housing over the last ten days. I met with them in their legislatives offices, in their communities, in the various regions and in the various provinces to explain the planned provisions respecting mortgage deferral. I explained the intentions of our government with respect to addressing tight rental markets. I wanted to receive input from the provincial ministers as to how these plans would meet the problems they might have identified and priorized in their regions.
This morning I had the opportunity to meet with the hon. Neil Windsor from Newfoundland. Although I had previously visited his province on a trip to see the maritime ministers, he was not there. However, this morning Mr. Windsor indicated that if the rental supply program responded to his particular market, it would be a welcome program. He indicated that the mortgage renewal plan had what he felt were shortcomings. He would have preferred a program lasting longer than one year.
As many hon. members have done, he also commented on the fact that the program calls for people to use the equity in their homes to deal with the problem of high interest rates at renewal time. I think I have addressed that problem. The design of the government is to have a modest program to help Canadians help themselves in these abnormal times.
In a budget which shows a reduction in the deficit next year of some $3 billion and under a very controlled program of government expenditures, why did the Minister of Finance commit $350 million toward these housing initiatives? Unfortunately the Conservative housing critic is not in the House this evening.

Mr. Speaker, these are the facts, and I shall come to them in a few moments.
I listened to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bus-sieres) this afternoon. What did he say? Inflation must be opposed. He did not use that famous, immortal phrase of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who said a few years ago that we have wrestled inflation to the ground. No, he did not say that. Inflation is the main enemy. We must beat inflation. He argued that the government is opposed to an expansionist policy. It has adopted a gradual first approach. In order to fight inflation, the government will have to cut back on the levels of goods and services that it provides. Next year's rate of growth for government expenditures will be reduced to 11.5 per cent, which the minister pointed out, quite correctly, will be less than the rate of inflation. In other words, the minister is admitting that we will have at least 12 per cent inflation. That is a great thing for the Canadian people to look forward to!
We have heard these arguments before. We have heard these arguments in the 1930s. What is the response of the Conservatives? They want more cutbacks and greater restraint. I think they should both look at a very interesting situation which happened a couple of weeks ago. We had an election in the province of Manitoba. For the first time in the history of Manitoba a government was not re-elected.
The reasons for that are pretty obvious. The Conservative government that was elected in 1977 pledged to the people of Manitoba that it would be a government of restraint, that it would cut back on the activities of government and it would let the free enterprise system run its natural course. It would free the free enterprise system from the heavy hand of government. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, they cut back all the programs one can think of. They cut back on daycare programs; they cut back on programs for senior citizens; they cut back on programs for native people; they cut back on hospitals; they cut back on pharmacare. The people of Manitoba had four years to look at this. They said, "We do not want this". Therefore, they did not re-elect the Conservative government. That Conservative government believed and adopted the same kind of policies that the Thatcher government later adopted in Great Britain and which President Reagan has adopted in the United States. Those governments, in Great Britain and in the United States, will suffer the same fate as the Conservative govern-

ment of Manitoba because people are not prepared to accept those kinds of conditions.
What is the policy of this government? The policy of the government has been very well explained by the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I have tried very hard during my years as a Member of Parliament not to deal with individual people but to deal with policies. I should like to say publicly, Mr. Speaker, that it comes with ill grace from the Governor of the Bank of Canada who has his office in an $80 million glass tower, who was receiving a salary of $95,000 a year and who in the last week or so received a 10 per cent increase. For him to lecture the ordinary people of this country and to tell them that they have to pull in their belts and that they will have to do without in order to beat inflation is saying, "Do as I say, not do as I do". I think that the people of Canada deserve better than they are getting from the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Bouey is the Governor of the Bank of Canada because this Liberal government and the short-lived Conservative government wanted him there. They wanted him there because they believe the policies which he implemented and in which he believes, are the right policies. What are those policies? The Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance believe in those policies, even though it is obvious to everyone, except the governor, that the high interest rates that we have at the present time are driving us further into a recession. They have destroyed the construction industry; they are destroying the automobile industry; they have destroyed the farm equipment industry. But the Governor of the Bank of Canada believes, despite all the evidence that we have, that in order to get out of this recession and to beat inflation we will have to keep the interest rates high. He claims that this is necessary in order to fight inflation. He says that this is just a difficult period of transition and that it is needed in order to lower inflation. Again, I say that it is other people who will have the difficult period and not the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
A few days ago, in a speech he made in Montreal he said that we are in a weaker economic phase and that it does not mean that we should stop worrying about our underlying problem of high inflation and concern ourselves solely with the immediate problem of unsatisfactory economic growth over the near term. Then he said that present interest levels, the bank prime lending rates and the mortgage rates are at about 17 per cent and that this only looks high compared with past levels. If one has to buy a house and one is earning $100,000 a year, one can live with a 17 per cent or a 20 per cent interest rate. The continued high interest rate policy will do two things. It will add to the inflationary pressures in the economy and it will reinforce inflationary expectations. Any worker faced with a 12 per cent inflation who has any ability to negotiate his wages, will ask for a 12 per cent increase to enable him to hold his own and stay where he is. It will also cut deeper into our economic production, close down factories and throw workers out of work.

He suggested that somehow we are akin to a communist party. If the hon. member wants to know what kind of socialist party we are, he should look at the socialist government of France. pension benefits in France. This is the kind of party we are. We are happy to be associated with the present government of France.
Let me turn to what I think is the most serious problem in the country, the fact that, according to Statistics Canada, in October 1981 the number of unemployed was 989,000. This was an increase of more than a 100,000 over the same period in 1980. The seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment was 8.3 per cent, an increase of eight-tenths of a percentage point over the same period last year. I wish the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean were present because he would know that the number of unemployed in the province of Quebec in the month of October was 320,000. That is a disgrace.
We must keep in mind that those figures do not tell the entire story. Between October and November in the province of Quebec 69,000 people disappeared from the labour force. They found that it was useless to look for work, and they just stopped looking for it. Once they stopped looking for work, they were not included on the list of unemployed because the figures of Statistics Canada are based on people who are not only unemployed but who are actively seeking work. There was no point in looking for work, so close to 150,000 people across Canada disappeared from the labour force. We have often talked about more than one million people being unemployed. Some hon. members of the House on both sides, depending upon whether they are in government or in opposition when they make the argument, frequently hear from professors who have good positions with tenure and fairly decent salaries and from some newspaper editorial writers who say that being unemployed is not very serious because there are unemployment insurance and welfare programs. They indicate, for example, that if a husband is not working his wife is, and that people are really not hurt or are trying to look for work.
During the Christmas-New Year's break last year I took the opportunity to meet some of the unemployed people in my constituency in an attempt to discover just what it meant to be unemployed. I should like to put a couple of illustrations on the record. First, 1 met a 57-year old man had worked for a milling company for 35 years; he never had another job. At the time the plant closed down he was earning about $8.61 per hour or $344 per week. His union had negotiated a good severance agreement, so he received one week's pay for each year that he worked, or approximately $12,000. Of course he received his unemployment insurance benefits, but his pension plan was not very good; his pension was very small. Let us assume that the severance pay and unemployment insurance would carry him fairly reasonably for a year. At age 58 he would be left with virtually nothing until he reached the age of 65 when he qualified for old age pension and the Canada Pension Plan. I should like one of the ministers to rise and explain to this man what he should and could do until he reaches age 65. The job opportunities for a man who is 57 or 58 years old are virtually nil.

For taxpayers in the $50,000-575,000 income group, the government will take an additional $105.6 million, but will lose $191,125,000. This means a net gain for this income class of $85,525,000.
In other words, the minister proposes to take from the middle class and give it to the rich. I wonder how many of these rich people live in the constituencies of the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond or the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimai'el). The council states further:
When we consider all taxpayers earning $40,000 or more, 98 per cent of the increased federal taxes resulting from the budget are redistributed within the same income category.
While there is some equity in eliminating tax advantages that do not apply equally to all income groups, we must question the wisdom of this expenditure of tax revenues. For these upper income categories, the government is giving a whopping handout of $735 million, which is
-almost half of the current federal contribution to provincial and municipal welfare programs;
-almost as much as the proposed cutback of funds to health and post-secondary education;	#
-and which by comparison would be enough to increase the Child Tax Credit by about $200, which would give additional assistance to Canada's working poor.
This is the analysis of the budget, in just a few sentences, of an organization which is not political or radical but which

represents people who work with the people in Canada who need assistance because they are sick or old or poor.
Again and again we are told by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, "We cannot afford it", and we are asked, "What do you propose?" One of the simple proposals which we have made is that the government receive a good part of the money from those who have it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addressing the motion of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), I should first want to note that few among us would argue that Canada is somehow immune from the inflation and other economic ills which have overtaken every western industrialized country. Indeed, Canada, with its heavy reliance on its export trade for its prosperity, is particularly vulnerable to the adverse economic developments that we have seen elsewhere in an increasingly interdependent international marketplace. If one considers the economic situations of our trading partners and other industrialized countries, Canada is to be seen in an enviable position. Nevertheless, there are obvious economic challenges facing Canadians today. They require a determined effort on the part of all sectors of our economy to overcome them.
While it is true that world circumstances have a major impact on our economy, there are things we can do at home to meet the economic challenges, and the government is doing them. For example, the government has concluded energy agreements with the western producing provinces. Those agreements provide not only a promising climate for massive

December 10, 1981
High Interest Rates
investment in the oil and gas sector, but they will also bring benefits for the economy as a whole, including the manufacturing sectors.
We have recently forged a made-in-Canada Constitution which, among other things, will provide for the free flow of goods, services, capital and labour which are so essential to a strong and vital common market. We have also tabled a budget which is committed to overcoming the root cause of our present economic problems, namely, inflation. The budget is not a quick fix. It is a determined effort to minimize the difficult economic challenges we, as Canadians, face in the near future. At the same time, it will maximize our economic potential in the medium and longer term.
It would seem, judging from the motion of the hon. member, that some hon. members opposite have neglected to consider the broad economic benefits provided by the energy agreements reached with the governments of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. Those agreements have created the underpinnings for our economic strategy for the decades ahead. Those accords not only provide for the further development of the petroleum sector, but for many other sectors throughout Canada as well. Indeed, the enormous economic spin-offs from the petroleum sector will provide for the greatest wave of capital investment in our history. Recent projections place investment at $1.5 trillion over the next decade, the great majority of which can be generated here in Canada.
We want all Canadians to share in the benefits and the economic opportunities of those accords. Accordingly, it was necessary not only to encourage Canadians to invest in their own petroleum sector, but also to strengthen the basic structure of our economic union. That, too, has now been accomplished with the approval of a made-in-Canada Constitution with a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The social and political ramifications of the charter are more obvious than its economic ramifications of that charter. Those economic elements will do much to ensure that all Canadians in the future have the opportunity to share in the material benefits of our economic growth. The charter provides for a national common market unhampered by artificial internal barriers erected by regions or by provincial governments. The charter encourages the free flow of goods, services, capital and labour which are so essential if we are to maximize our true economic potential. The new Constitution does something more. It also provides investors with a more stable and understandable economic environment. This reassurance of our economic union will, in turn, create a higher degree of investment and provide more jobs and opportunities for all.
The realization of our full economic potential and the resolution of many of our current economic challenges can be achieved when large capital investment is matched with greater productivity and more sourcing of Canadian goods and services. The new Constitution accordingly provides our business community with the assurance of a greater domestic market for its goods and services.
Underlying the energy agreements and the Charter of Rights is the concept of sharing and the belief that all Canadians, from every province and territory, have the right to share in the benefits which both nature and technology have bestowed upon us. The more equitable distribution of Canada's vast wealth among all regions has been a goal of this government, and it continues to be a goal in the economic program submitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) earlier in this session. However, equity is only one aspect of our total economic program.
If one is to appreciate fully the broad elements of the government's commitment to meet the economic challenges now confronting Canadians, one must consider its fundamental objectives. The most important of these objectives is our pledge to reduce inflation. We cannot be satisfied with living with inflation. Such complacency will only hinder growth and create more unemployment. The recent budget abjures piecemeal measures. This is seen in the budget's commitment to match monetary restraint, that is, restraint in the growth of the money supply and credit, with a greater measure of fiscal restraint, including federal government spending.
In recent years, members opposite have strongly criticized the government for what they called fiscal irresponsibility, deploring in particular budget deficits. Such members were quick to argue that the budget deficit had to be reduced significantly if inflation were to be brought under control. Accordingly, I find it strange that these same critics, who now attack the budget, have suddenly forgotten what to them was, only a short time ago, so important.
Fiscal restraint proposed in the budget is part of the government's commitment to reduce deficit spending. Measures included in the budget will reduce the government's borrowing requirements from almost $10 billion this year to $6.6 billion in 1982-1983. The budgetary deficit is projected to drop from about $15 billion to about $10 billion over the same period. This reduction in such a short period is substantial. It will contribute in a major way to strengthening the government's financial position which, in turn, should relieve the pressure on capital markets and thus contribute to lower interest rates for both corporate and private investors. This objective will be reinforced through increased revenues deriving from energy agreements and a more equitable structure in our tax system.
The belief in the soundness of the government's attempt to reduce inflation through a balanced application of restraint on expenditure and some increase in revenue is shared by many Canadians. For example, a recent article in The Globe and Mail stated:
Finance Minister Allan MacEachen's budget was a good one. Its broad strategy is fundamentally sound. A greater degree of fiscal restraint can indeed take some of the pressure off monetary policy and interest rates in resisting inflation and pave the way for future growth.
The government shares the concern of all Canadians during the current period of sluggish international economic growth. However, there is no alternative that would produce better
December 10, 1981

short term results without harming the medium and long-term prospects for sustained growth in our economy.
Concern over the short term has prompted some to question the desirability of pursuing a policy of deficit reduction at present because of the danger of accentuated recession. Such critics argue that if one takes into account distortions introduced by inflation and the fact that revenues of the provincial and the national governments together are in surplus, there is no need for deficit reduction.
Superficially, that argument is attractive, relying on a basic Keynesian belief that fiscal policy should be the chief element in the government's arsenal for managing short term output and employment. Our budget strategy is, however, more farsighted. It is based on the belief that fiscal and monetary policy working together can produce sound economic performance with regard to inflation and its concomitant of unemployment.
Certainly, we must be realistic about the present economic situation when deciding what approach to adopt. It is clear that inflation remains a long-term problem. It cannot be reduced quickly. There are too many international pressures and too much built-in inertia in the inflationary process itself for that to happen. Therefore, while proposing certain shortterm remedial measures to help those most in need, the government is creating the circumstances for medium to longterm future growth for a stronger, more stable economy.
The government has had to work under considerable limitations in developing such economic strategy. Essentially, the question is how best to resist an increase in inflation without at the same time committing the economy to a deep, prolonged recession. The federal government deficit reduction is clearly a fundamental element of an over-all strategy best suited to meet this difficult dilemma.
National economic renewal, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has asserted, is the overriding priority of this government. "Economic renewal must be accomplished within the restraints required to reduce inflation", as he has noted. Indeed, if Canadians are to reap the tremendous opportunities for growth and development in all regions, we must reduce inflation as well as to increase investment, modernization and development.
The federal government has an important leadership role to play in managing and exploiting opportunities and ensuring that the benefits are shared equally by all Canadians. The government, as part of its over-all fiscal plan, is allocating $42 billion to economic development and over $18 billion to energy development over the next five years.
There are many large capital projects planned for the next two decades. The recent major projects task force, composed of business and labour representatives, estimated that the total value of identified projects is approximately $500 billion to the year 2000. Projects in the field of industrial development, resource development, the transport of bulk commodities and export promotion, all hold great promise for our economic future. The savings made through the pursuit of a policy of
High Interest Rates
deficit reduction and fiscal restraint will find countless outlets for productive use.
As the paper on "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s", included in the budget documents, states:
Close co-operation between governments, business and labour will be needed to permit Canada to develop the industrial capacity to build the machinery and other products needed for resource development in Canada and abroad.
For example, a private sector export trade development board has been created to give the business community a greater opportunity to contribute to the formulation of trade policy, a major priority in the government's current economic strategy. And seeking greater co-operation between the public sector and the private sector, the government is also committed to a careful examination of our regulatory systems to ensure that the rules are clear and the procedures efficient so that they guide business enterprise rather than inhibit it.
We also seek in our economic planning to overcome the mismatch between skills and available jobs which has emerged as a key constraint on economic development and a serious problem for working Canadians. As the budget notes, as the pattern of economic activity changes so does the availability of job opportunities in terms of both their location and their skill requirements. Here is a challenge for greater consultation and co-operation between the public and private sectors. The result of these and other initiatives will be a stronger, investment-led economy, yet one which is more internationally competitive. I would ask hon. members opposite whether this is not preferable to an economy with an over-extended current account deficit paralleling a large federal deficit. This is why the economic program announced by the Minister of Finance is sound and, in the circumstances, the most sensible for dealing with our current economic challenges.
Clearly Canada, like all western industrialized economies, faces difficult economic decisions. In many respects Canada is, indeed, in an enviable position with its enormous resource and industrial potential. However, our sheer territorial size, our small population, the distances to markets and our reliance on export trade pose many difficulties to our growth. Nevertheless, our economic future is bright.
As I have noted, we have set the essential foundation for sustained economic growth by reaching energy accords with the western producing provinces. The direct and spin-off effects of those agreements will set the stage for massive new investment in Canada. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms as part of the Constitution creates a true common market, an economic union which provides for the free flow of goods, services, capital and labour, unrestricted by internal barriers. That move will help to ensure that all productive factors are used as efficiently as possible.
The budget attempts to take advantage of our basic strengths. It does so by promoting a balanced application of spending restraint and increase in revenue. The necessary restraint required to reduce the federal deficit so as to counter

December 10, 1981
High Interest Rates
the forces of inflation and to promote economic growth is being broadly shared by government, business and private individuals to ensure a healthy economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take no pleasure in joining my colleagues to speak to this motion. I support the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) in the motion which states:
That this House censures the government for its perpetual, excessive, and ineffective reliance on a high interest rate policy, which has not only created the worst economic recession in Canada since the 1930s, but which also continues to threaten the survival of thousands of small enterprises, adds more Canadians daily to the ranks of the million already out of work, and confronts home owners and renters alike with the worst housing crisis since the Second World War.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) rose in the House earlier this evening and said this is not the worst crisis we have had, and he mentioned other years when we had worse crises. I do not care whether it is the worst crisis, all I know is that it is a terrible crisis in relation to housing, inflation, interest rates and unemployment, yet the Minister of Public Works can quibble over whether this is the worst crisis we have had since the thirties.
On December 3 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated in Toronto that the blame for high interest rates lies with the banks, the market economy and individuals who want good returns on Canada Savings Bonds, not with his government. This Prime Minister never takes the blame for things he does. Who controls interest rates in Canada? Are they controlled by the market economy, by individuals or by the banks? Surely there is not one person in the House who believes that any of these can control interest rates. Only the Bank of Canada can control interest rates, and the government controls the Bank of Canada. There is no question as to who is controlling rates and stopping those interest rates from coming down. Anyone with any experience in the marketplace or who has been in the investment business can tell you that the Bank of Canada is controlling the treasury bill rate.
If the government believes the banks are responsible, then let them release the banks from the regulation that prevents them from moving interest rates down freely. I challenge the government to do that. I challenge the Bank of Canada, through the government, to get out of the treasury bill market and find out how fast interest rates will come down. They would come down very fast. The banks do not like the rates going up and down. Anyone in the finance industry will tell you that any financial institution needs steady rates. They do not care what the rates are, how high or how low; it is the spread between deposits and loans that is important. Unfortunately the government continues to spread the big lie that the banks are solely responsible.
No one is innocent, but the banks are not solely responsible. It is the Bank of Canada that is mainly responsible. Everyone knows that the Bank of Canada can drop interest rates if that is desired, but not the chartered banks. The chartered banks take their cue from the Bank of Canada and no one else.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said in the House today that he had the support of the House for his budget. If he had said he had the support of the majority of
the House, the Liberal members, that would have been a valid statement, but to stand up here and say he had the support of the House is ridiculous.
The Minister of Finance said that interest rates are going to come down and the government is going to beat inflation. Quite frankly we know they are not, because he said in the budget what he expects. All one has to do is to read the budget which says that the government expects interest rates to come down by 1 per cent per year over the next four years. That is what the government expects, and that is what the average person out there is faced with. That is what the average person has to contend with over the next four years-more high interest rates.
We may not have the worst economic recession since the 1930s, but it is awfully close. We are not going to argue whether it is the worst, but I do not want to see anything worse than this. Some 140,000 Canadians have lost their jobs in the last short while and 50,000 have stopped looking for work. There are almost a million people in Canada out of work.
Let me put to rest once and for all the question as to whether the Prime Minister cares. Twenty-eight years ago when the Minister of Finance came to the House of Commons, the average unemployment rate in his riding was 25 per cent. Today, 28 years later, the average unemployment rate is still 25 per cent. Let him stand and deny that. He would not dare. He keeps getting elected by giving special grants in his riding, and he has been doing that for years. Any member who does not agree, let him please stand up.
What has this government offered small business? The minister says he is offering something to small business. At page five of the budget he said that abnormally high interest rates have had a particularly adverse effect on many small businesses. So what does he do? He guts the Small Business Development Bond. He extends it for one more year, but the only way that businessmen can get it is if they are going bankrupt or their business is failing. After these businessmen go to the banks or to the FBDB and are not able to get any money, they finally go to the government and apply for a Small Business Development Bond. The Minister of Finance, being as generous as he always is, says they can have the Small Business Development Bond at an excellent rate of interest.
But what does the budget say about the rate of interest? Under the former provisions of the Small Business Development Bond, money could be borrowed at one half of prime plus up to 3 per cent, based on the marginal tax rate of the particular bank. For example, if the prime rate is 18 per cent and you borrow from the Small Business Development Bond, it would be 9 per cent. Based on the marginal tax rate of the bank, you could be borrowing at a rate of 10 per cent, 11 per cent or 12 per cent. Under the provisions of the budget, the deal that the minister is now offering sets out that if, for example, the prime rate is 18 per cent, you must subtract 6 per cent because the banks will be taxed on that. The rate is back down to 12 per cent, and half of that is taken away, leaving 6
December 10, 1981

per cent. The other 6 per cent on which the banks will be taxed is added back on to bring the rate back to 12 per cent. Based on the marginal tax rate of the bank, one per cent is added to that, and it is back to 12 per cent, 13 per cent or 14 per cent. In effect, what the minister has done and is afraid to admit is that he has not only gutted the Small Business Development Bond, he has raised the interest rates on it by 2 per cent. He does not have the courage to stand up in the House and say that that is what he has done.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen are up in arms, and why not? The government will never again get support from that association. All that business will do is to march to Ottawa when the government passes legislation to plead with the government to roll back certain provisions of the legislation. They have to take this course of action with this budget.
Thousands of letters are being sent to the government from the small insurance companies which say that the government is driving them out of business. But the government does not care. The companies are lining up to try to get concessions. What does the Minister of Finance do about this situation? Of all things, he offers jobs to a group of unemployed miners from Cape Breton in Fernie, B.C. in February of 1982. They accepted that offer on the condition that they get a housing subsidy from the employer, and the employer agreed. Now these miners are telling the employer that perhaps they do not want to move because that subsidy becomes a taxable benefit. All the minister can say is that he will consider that problem.
The housing requirement in Canada is for 220,000 units. Until recently we expected to have 170,000 units for 1981. This is a shortfall of 50,000 units. We have now discovered that CMHC projects that the number of completed units for 1981 and into 1982 may be as small as 135,000. The government says it has a solution for this also. It will provide a benefit of $350 million to ease the crisis. When this figure is dissected, we find that $150 million is provided for the first year and $200 million for the second year. The government will provide an interest-free loan of $7,500 for 15,000 rental units, and this figure of $112 million must be subtracted from the $150 million. That leaves $38 million for home owners who are in trouble. This means that 13,000 people in Canada can receive assistance for their mortgages from the government this year. The statistics suggest that over 900,000 people are renewing their mortgages, and CMHC statistics reveal that one in 11 will have difficulty in paying his mortgage, but yet only 13,000 will be helped.
Of the 220,000 units needed in Canada, 110,000 are rental units. What is this government offering? It is offering help to 13,000 people. The Minister of Finance and other Liberals continue to say that they will help Canadians, but they are providing no help. The vacancy rates in many parts of Canada are zero. The minister stood up in the House to say that he would extend the MURBs, and then in a whisper he said, "until December 31, 1981." The minister is obviously not aware that many investors in rental housing require up to eight years to recover their investment. The soft costs were not
High Interest Rates
important until the interest rates went up to a critical 13 per cent, 14 per cent or more. The soft costs were of exceptional benefit to those investors who were building rental units, but the Minister of Finance introduced his budget in isolation. He now says he would like to consult with business after the fact.

In 1973, the government said that inflation was beaten. However, it is still with us. In 1975, the Bank of Canada said it had solved the problem of high interest rates and that it would control the money supply to prevent the problem of high interest rates. That has not been solved. In 1973, the government said that Canada would have oil self-sufficiency. We do not have it. The government indicated in 1974 that government spending would be under control. Some control! This government ship has so many leaks that if it becomes unshoaled, it will sink fast and deep. The only way for it to survive is to remain on the shoal.
It is my intention to support the motion which was moved by my hon. friend from St. John's East. Hopefully the government will come to its senses and remedy the mistakes pointed out in the motion. speechtext:
Then, as my colleague says, they voted for the budget. And what a budget! The Minister of Finance stood in the House and said he would not withdraw the budget. He said he might make some changes if we pleaded with him. If we beg, he might make some changes, but will he be like the Minister of Public Works, who said that if people send him letters and telephone him, he will help them with their problems? The Minister of Public Works sent letters to hon. members on this side of the House saying that he would not provide assistance to people who are having trouble. He told us to wait for the budget. In order to do that, we have to consult with business before the deed is done and not after. We must consult before rather than after the budget.

This budget has been formulated by a group of civil servants. The minister must stand up and answer for that. He and other ministers must stand up and defend the budget, but they do not know how to defend it. It is a terrible budget to have to defend. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), a couple of good Tories, are proposing that this government reduce interest rates. speechtext:
They are back with a brand new show appropriately dubbed the Tory interest rate magic. And boy, is it a winner! It is a seat filler. This time they have something for everybody. Do you have a problem meeting your mortgage payment? Don't worry about it; the Tories have the answer. Are you having trouble carrying inventory in your business? Relax; the Tories have just what you need. They have the Tory interest rate magic. They have your problem all figured out.
Or have they? Did they bother to tell the people of Canada that the people on this side of the House have mortgages too? We too would dearly love to see the interest rate reduced a few percentage points. I am sure the Tories have told the people that this government has the power to reduce interest rates, today or tomorrow morning, to 12 per cent, 10 per cent or 8 per cent, but did they bother to tell the people of Canada some of the consequences of such a decision? Did they happen to tell us about the people who own the money, the investors? Perhaps those investors might just put their money where they get the greatest return on it? If an investor can invest his or her money in Canada at, say, 10 per cent or in the United States at 16 per cent or 18 per cent, where is he or she going to put it?
I have a mortgage too. It is due in February, and as it now stands, my bank manager is going to say to me either "I have some good news for you" or "I have some bad news for you". The good news will be that the interest rate is down a percentage point or two since last February, or the bad news will be that it is up a percentage point or two. He will also say he can lend me money for my house at the present rate, if I am willing to pay that rate. He will have the money. However, let us suppose the United States rate remains high. Let us also suppose that this government decides today or tomorrow morning to reduce interest rates to 10 per cent or 12 per cent so that the Canadian rate would be substantially below the American rate. Imagine my situation in February when I walk into my bank manager's office to try to renew my mortgage. He would probably say to me that he has some good news and some bad news. The good news would be that the mortgage rate has dropped several percentage points. It would not be 16.75 per cent as it was last year; it would be down to 10 per cent. That would be good news, but then he would go on and tell me the bad news. The bad news would be that he does not have any money to lend. He would go on and tell me the reasons, which would be quite straightforward and easy to figure out. The investors who own the money would have taken their money to where they could make the most on it and where they could get the greatest return. They would have taken it out of the country to where the interest rate is higher, and that would be to the United States.
If I were asked whether I wanted a high interest rate or a low interest rate, my answer would be easy: of course I want a low interest rate. I am a mortgage holder too. I want a low rate, and so does every mortgage holder in the country. However, if my choice is renewing my mortgage or not renewing it and if my choice is keeping my house or not keeping it, that is really not a choice at all. Like every other mortgage holder in the country, I want to be able to renew my mortgage, which means that there will have to be money available for that purpose. It will not be available if the investor has taken his or her money to the United States where he or she can get a higher rate of return.

I remember as far back as 1958 or 1959 when the hon. member for St. John's East was first elected to the House of Commons. He was on the radio almost every day in Newfoundland, and he became known as one of the great consumer advocates of Newfoundland. People used to say, whatever their partisan affiliation, if that member ever gets in government, he is going to do great things for the consumer because he has such a grasp of the issues. He talked about the kinds of programs children were exposed to over television. He talked about all kinds of consumer issues.
I watched when he got into government, as he did ever so briefly. I watched him and the Tory record for nine months. The record clearly shows that this gentleman, the mover of this resolution, my fellow Newfoundlander from St. John's East, did not, in his brief term in government, take one single initiative to address any of the consumer concerns he fought for for 20 years before he got into cabinet. There was not one issue, not one tittle, not one bit of legislation, not one item during the time he was in cabinet that he addressed. Therefore, we put the lie to his crusading. He is great on words and he is long on words, as he is in this resolution. However, he is terribly short on action when he gets in a position where he can do something about it.
I want to refer my good friends, whose blood pressure is rising unjustifiably, to another of their friends in a very friendly fashion. I am going to talk about their finance spokesman, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). We on this side think this man really has his head screwed on right. I refer to his interview in the November 7 edition of the Financial Post. I ask those on the Tory side of the House, the permanent opposition, to compare the spirit of that interview with the spirit of the resolution moved by the hon. member for St. John's East. I submit they are mutually exclusive. One says one thing and the other says the opposite. Here in the public record is the finance spokesman for the Tory party as being
High Interest Rates
largely in support of the interest rate policy pursued by the Bank of Canada at this time. I refer to the Financial Post of November 7.
If that is not enough, let us put all the Tory Newfoundlanders together. Let us look at what my good friend, the junior member from Newfoundland, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the one-time Tory finance critic, had to say. He conceded outside the House that Canadian interest rates "will have to follow to some degree" rates in the United States. He said that in November, 1980. That was at another time when he had another incarnation. He was still wearing the finance hat. That was before his demotion to other matters. When the hon. member for St. John's West was still speaking for the Tory party on this issue, he was saying that we have to follow the United States interest rate. That, in essence, is what I have said tonight, not that we do it anxiously, happily or with any degree of satisfaction. We do it because we do not believe in fooling the people of Canada into thinking we can live in glass houses, bury our heads in the sand, ignore what is going on around us, ignore our trade relations with the United States, ignore that we live on a continent which has a very densely populated country many times the population of ours. We do not pretend to the Canadian people that we can somehow have artificial solutions to the problems we face in this country.
We have levelled with the Canadian people. We have been responsible to the Canadian people. I say to my hon. friend from St. John's East that this resolution is dishonest. For that reason I and members on this side will defeat it.
